**﴿Alif-Lam-Mim﴾**

If it is made the name of the surah or of the Qur'an, then its place in i'rab (grammatical parsing) is nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "This is Alif-Lam-Mim." His saying, ﴿The revelation of the Book﴾, is a second predicate, taking the verbal noun (*masdar*) in its original sense for the purpose of emphasis (mubalaghah), or with an elided modifier (mudaf) understood, or it is interpreted as the passive participle, meaning "revealed (munazzal)." Its annexation to "the Book" is the annexation of an attribute to the thing described, or it is explanatory, in the sense of "from (min)." His saying, glorified be He, ﴿there is no doubt in it﴾ is a third predicate, and His saying, exalted be He, ﴿from the Lord of the worlds﴾ is a fourth predicate. It is also permitted that "Alif-Lam-Mim" be the subject, and what follows be its predicates, meaning: "The one named Alif-Lam-Mim is the Book revealed, in which there is no doubt, from the Lord of the worlds." This has been objected to on the ground that what is made the title of a subject should, before that, be known to be attributed to it, and since there is no prior established attribution, its attributions should be stated as news.

Abu al-Baqa' said: "Alif-Lam-Mim" may be the subject, with *tanzil* in the sense of *munazzal* as its predicate; *la rayba fihi* ("there is no doubt in it") is a circumstantial clause (hal) of *al-kitab* ("the Book"), its governing element being the annexed noun, and it is an emphatic circumstance; *min Rabbi* ("from the Lord") is connected to *tanzil*. It is also permitted that it be connected to an omitted element, which is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in *fihi* ("in it"), its governing element being the adverbial phrase, not *rayba* ("doubt"), because here *rayb* is indeclinable (mabni), and in it is what you have heard. This connection is also permitted on the assumption that *Alif-Lam-Mim* is the predicate of an omitted subject, and what follows is predicates of that omitted subject. If *Alif-Lam-Mim* is taken as listed in a series of enumeration, it has no place in i'rab. There are several possibilities for what follows. Abu al-Baqa' said: It is permitted that *tanzil* be the subject, *la rayba fihi* the predicate, *min Rabbi* a circumstantial clause as stated above, and on this it is not permitted to connect it to *tanzil*, because the verbal noun has already been given as the predicate about it. It is also permitted that the predicate be *min Rabbi*, and *la rayba* a circumstantial clause of *al-kitab*, and that it be a second predicate after a predicate. End of quotation.

The reason for prohibiting the connection to the verbal noun after it has been made the predicate is that it is a weak governing element, so its governance does not extend to what follows the predicate. Against the requirement of the hadith on expanding the adverbial phrase, there is latitude here, or the element connected is part of the complete meaning, and a noun is not predicated about before its completion. Ibn 'Atiyyah permitted connecting *min Rabbi* to *rayb* ("doubt"), but this is far from the intended meaning. al-Hufi permitted *tanzil* to be the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "What is composed of the kind mentioned is the revelation of the Book." Abu Hayyan said: "What I choose is that *tanzil* be the subject, *la rayba fihi* a parenthetical insertion with no place in i'rab, and *min Rabbi al-'alamin* the predicate. The pronoun in *fihi* refers to the content of the sentence, namely its being sent down from the Lord of the worlds, not to the revelation or to the Book, as if it were said: 'There is no doubt in that,' that is, in its being sent down from the Lord of the worlds." This is what al-Zamakhshari relied upon, and he mentioned that it is the preferred view. Its soundness is supported by the saying of God, exalted be He:

﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"?﴾ For their saying this is a fabrication. It is a denial that it could be from the Lord of the worlds. That is, the more fitting reading is that the negation of doubt applies to what they denied, namely that it is from the Lord of the worlds, exalted is His majesty. It has also been said: that is, it is necessary that its subject be a judgment intended for the sake of informing, not a qualifier of the judgment by the negation of doubt concerning it. In this there is a discussion. Likewise His words, glorified is He: ﴿Rather, it is the truth from your Lord﴾, for it is an affirmation of what precedes it, so it is like it in testimony. Then he said, regarding the composition of the speech on this: it is a sound, firm style, in which He, glorified is He, first affirmed that its sending down is from the Lord of the worlds, and that this is something in which there is no doubt. That is, there is no room for doubt that it is the sending down of God, exalted is He, and doubt is the furthest thing from it, because the one who negates doubt and removes it together with it is never separated from it at all, namely that it is inimitable for mankind. Then, exalted is He, turned away from that to His words, exalted is He: "Or do they say, 'He has invented it'?" For "am" here is the disjunctive "am" which means "rather," and the interrogative hamza is for denial of their saying and for expressing wonder at it, because the incapacity of their eloquent ones to produce the like of even the shortest surah of it is manifest. So it is either the saying of a contentious, obstinate person, or of an ignorant one from whom the eyes are blinded. Then, glorified is He, turned from denial to affirming that it is the truth from your Lord. There is also a goodness in choosing the word "the truth" and defining it as the definite of genus. Close to this view, in my opinion, is making "sending down" the subject, and the clause "there is no doubt in it" in the position of a circumstantial clause for "the Book," with "from the Lord" as the predicate, so reflect on this, and do not be heedless. Abu 'Ubayda claimed that "am" means "bal" of transition, and said: this is a leaving of one discourse for another, and it is nothing.

The apparent reading is that "from your Lord" is in the position of a circumstantial clause, meaning existing from your Lord. It has been said that it is permissible to make it a second predicate. The addition of "Lord" to "the worlds" first, then to the pronoun of the master of those addressed, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, second, after what it contains of the goodness of transition to the affirmation of prophethood and the magnification of his station, exalted is his station in it, that he, upon him be blessings and peace, is the all-comprehensive servant who gathered what was scattered in the world by being a prisoner. Its occurrence in the style of ascent indicates that his comprehensiveness, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, is more complete than that of the entire world, and it is fitting for him, God's blessings and peace be upon him.

﴿That you may warn a people to whom no warner has come before you﴾ is an explanation of the purpose of its sending down. It has been said that it is connected to "sending down." It has been said that it is connected to an omitted element, that is, He sent it down so that you may warn, etc. It has also been said that it is connected to what is connected to "from your Lord." "A people" is the first object of "to warn," and the second object is omitted, that is, the punishment. "Ma" is a negation, as is apparent. The first "min" is extra, "nadhir" is the subject of "atahum," and it is applied to the Messenger, which is the well-known meaning, and to what includes him, and to the scholar who warns on behalf of the Mighty and Majestic. It has been said that this is what is meant here, as in His words: ﴿And there is no nation but that a warner has passed among them﴾ [Fatir: 24].

It is permitted that "nadhir" here be a verbal noun meaning warning. "From before you" means from before your warning or from before your time, and it is connected to "atahum." The clause is in the position of a qualifier of "a people." What is meant by them is Quraysh, according to what many have held. In al-Kashshaf he said: the apparent is that no messenger was sent to them from among them before the Messenger of God ﷺ, and they were obligated to the laws of the messengers before, although they were negligent in searching for them, especially the religion of Ibrahim and Isma'il, peace be upon them both, if we say that the calls of Musa and Isa, peace be upon them both, did not include them, and this is the more evident view. You have already had the statement on the cessation of the authority of the prophethood of every prophet other than our Prophet ﷺ after his death, so no one who comes after him is obligated absolutely to follow him, and the statement of cessation applies except in relation to those who were of his offspring. The apparent view is that Quraysh were obligated to the religion of Ibrahim and Isma'il, peace be upon them both, and that they continued upon that until the worship of idols, which 'Amr al-Khuza'i, may God curse him, introduced among them, spread among the Arabs, so that none remained upon the upright religion except a few, indeed fewer than a few. So they are included in the generality of His words: ﴿And there is no nation but that a warner has passed among them﴾, for it is general to the Messenger and to the scholar who warns. So it is said. It was raised as an objection together with what is here, and it was answered that what is meant here is that no warner from among them came to them before you, and the statement of al-Kashshaf points to this; and there it is "but a warner has passed among them," from them or from others, or the warner there is taken as a messenger and here in general. Abu Hayyan said in his commentary on Surah al-Malaika: the calling to God, exalted is He, has not ceased from every nation, either through direct contact from their prophets, or through transmission up to the time of the sending of Muhammad ﷺ. The verses which indicate that Quraysh had no warner come to them mean that he did not directly contact them and their nearest forefathers. Or the warning ceased and so was not general, when its effects began to fade, Muhammad ﷺ was sent. What the people of kalam have mentioned about the state of the people of the intervals is on the basis of supposition, not that it actually occurred, so there is not a nation on the face of the earth but that it knew the calling to God, exalted and mighty is He, and His worship, end of quotation.

There is something troubling in this, and its implication is that what is negated here is the coming of a direct warner, that is, a prophet of the prophets, peace be upon them, to Quraysh who were in his time, upon him be blessings and peace, before him, ﷺ, and that there was among them one who warned them and called them to the worship of God alone by transmission, that is, from a prophet who was calling to that. The first is something two people should not differ about, indeed no person should hesitate about it. The second is a presumed certainty in the case of Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl al-'Adawi, father of Sa'id, one of the Ten. For he was a contemporary of the Prophet ﷺ, met him, and believed in him before his mission, upon him be blessings and peace, but did not live to see it, as he died while Quraysh were rebuilding the Ka'ba, and that was five years before the mission, and he was upon the religion of Ibrahim and Isma'il, peace be upon them both. It is authentically transmitted from Hisham ibn 'Urwa, from his father, from Asma' bint Abi Bakr, who said: I saw Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl leaning his back against the Ka'ba, saying: "O assembly of Quraysh, by Him in whose hand is my soul, none of you is this morning upon the religion of Ibrahim except me." In some other transmissions of the report from him there is also an addition: he used to say, "O God, if I knew the most beloved of the forms by which You are to be worshipped, I would worship You by it, but I do not know," then he would prostrate on his mount. Musa ibn 'Uqba mentioned in al-Maghazi: I heard from one I trust who narrated that Zayd ibn 'Amr used to blame Quraysh for slaughtering for other than God, exalted is He. It is also authentic that he did not eat of the slaughtered animals of the polytheists over which other than God had been invoked.

Al-Tayalisi related in his Musnad from his son Sa'id, who said: "I said to the Prophet ﷺ: 'My father was as you saw and as has reached you, so shall I seek forgiveness for him?' He said: 'Yes, for he will be raised on the Day of Resurrection as a community alone.'"

It is not far-fetched for one whose condition was this to warn and call to the worship of God, exalted is He. Rather, whoever is fair sees in his statement, which Asma' related, and his denunciation of Quraysh for slaughtering to other than God, which al-Tayalisi mentioned, and his calling to the religion of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and the worship of God, glorified is He, alone, that this also includes transmission. From what we have quoted it is known that this man, may God be pleased with him, was not a prophet, which is evident. Some claimed that he was a prophet, and argued for that by his leaning his back against the Ka'ba and saying, "Come to me, for none remains upon the religion of the Friend except me." The soundness of that is disputed, and even if granted, there is no proof in it for the intended point, as is not hidden from anyone with the least discernment. Like Zayd, may God be pleased with him, is Qiss ibn Sa'ida al-Iyadi, for he, may God be pleased with him, was a believer in God, the Mighty and Majestic, calling to the worship of Him, glorified is He, alone.

Al-Alusi also notes that he was a contemporary of the Prophet ﷺ and died before the Prophethood, upon the Hanifiyya (the pure monotheistic creed of Abraham). He was among the long-lived, and al-Sijistani mentioned that he lived three hundred and eighty years. Al-Marzubani said: Many people of knowledge have mentioned that he lived six hundred years. Many reports have been related about his case, but al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar said in his book al-Isaba: Some narrators have devoted a separate chain to Qass, in which is his poetry and his sermon, in al-Tiwalat (the long narrations) of al-Tabarani and others, but all of its chains are weak, and he enumerated what he enumerated, so let it be consulted. Furthermore, the difficulty is only supposed if by Quraysh is meant all the descendants of Qusayy, or Fihr, or al-Nadr, or Ilyas, or Mudar. But if what is meant is those among them at the time he ﷺ was sent, then there is no difficulty, as will not be hidden from the reflective one, so reflect. It has also been said: the intended people are the Arabs, Quraysh and others, and there had not come to those of them contemporary with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ any warner from the prophets (peace be upon them) other than him ﷺ. There were among them those who warned and called to the Tawhid (oneness of God) and the worship of Allah alone, but he was not a prophet, as you have heard a moment ago. As for the Arabs who were not contemporary, there had not come to them, since the era of Isma'il (peace be upon him), any prophet from among them. Rather, no prophet at all had been sent to them. Musa, Isa and other prophets of the Children of Israel (peace be upon them) were not sent to them, according to the most apparent view. Khalid ibn Sinan al-Absi, according to most, is not a prophet. The report of an old daughter of his coming to the Prophet ﷺ, and his ﷺ saying to her: "Welcome, daughter of a prophet whom his people neglected," and similar reports, which the scholars of hadith have objections to, are not suitable for use as evidence. In the commentaries on al-Shifa and in al-Isaba of al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar there is some discussion of this. It has also been said: the intended people are the people of the interval (al-fatra) among the Arabs and others, even the People of the Book, and the meaning is: there had not come to them a warner before you, after the misguidance that occurred among them. This is it. And it seems to me that you take the warner here to be the Messenger who warns on behalf of Allah, azza wa jall, and likewise in His saying: ﴿And there is no nation but a warner has passed among them﴾, to agree with His saying: ﴿And We certainly sent into every nation a messenger, [saying], "Worship Allah"﴾ [al-Nahl: 36]. I think you make the tanwin in (ummah) for magnification, meaning: And there is no great nation, whose affair is cared for, but a warner has passed among it, and We certainly sent into every great nation whose affair is cared for a messenger. Or you consider the Arabs one nation and the Children of Israel another nation, and similar to that a nation below the people of one era. And you take "those to whom no warner came" to mean a group of a nation to whom no warner came specifically. Among what may be taken as support for this: when the coming of a warner is negated, it is negated of a people and the like, not of a nation, so reflect. The full discussion of this point will come, God willing, Most High. It has also been permitted that (ma) is a relative pronoun, functioning as the second object of (li-tundhira), and (min nadhir) is connected to (ataahum), meaning: that you warn a people of the punishment that came to them from a warner before you, i.e., through the tongue of a warner before you. Abu Hayyan chose this, and according to it there is no room for the supposition of the difficulty. But it is not hidden that this contradicts the apparent sense on which most exegetes rely. The restriction to warning in explaining the wisdom is because it is what is required by their saying "he has fabricated it" (iftarahu), not good news. ﴿So that they may be guided﴾: i.e., in order that they be guided by your warning them, or hoping for their guidance. Making the hope a metaphor for will, attributed to Him, azza wa jall, is a Mu'tazili tendency.

﴿Allah is He who created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, then established Himself upon the Throne﴾. Its explanation has passed earlier, according to the position of both the salaf (the early generations) and the khalaf (the later generations). ﴿You have no protector (waliyy) or intercessor (shafi') besides Him﴾. That is, you have no one who can surpass Allah, Mighty and Majestic, so that there is a protector or an intercessor, meaning: these two (protector and intercessor) from among the created beings cannot benefit you with Him, Glorified is He, without His pleasure, Exalted is His majesty. (*Min dunihi*) is a circumstantial phrase (hal) from the genitive pronoun in (*lakum*), and the governing element is the preposition or what it is attached to. On this meaning, the address contains no evidence that He, Exalted, is an intercessor to the exclusion of others, such that one might ask: how can that be, when it is too exalted for Him, Exalted is His dignity, to be an intercessor? Sufficient in this is his ﷺ rejection of the Bedouin when he said: "We seek intercession with Allah, Exalted, through you." It may also be said: what is impermissible is applying the term "intercessor" to Him, Exalted, in its literal meaning (haqiqi).

[Page 120]

As for applying it to Him, Glorified is He, in the sense of "helper" (nasir) in a figurative way (majaz), this is not impermissible, and it may be considered here. In that case (*min dunihi*) may be a circumstantial phrase relating to what follows it, which has been placed before it because it is indefinite (nakira). Here (*dun*) means (*ghayr*, "other than"), and the meaning is: you have no protector or helper other than Allah, Exalted. It may also be a circumstantial phrase from the genitive pronoun, as in the previous interpretation, and the meaning is: you have, if you exceed His guardianship and His support, Mighty and Exalted, no protector or helper. It appears to me that the expression "intercessor" here is by way of an implied (taqdiriyya) *mushakala* (a rhetorical association of terms), since the idolatrous warned ones often used to say of their gods, "These are our intercessors," and they claimed that each of them was an intercessor for them. ﴿Will you not then take heed?﴾ That is: do you not hear these admonitions so that you take heed from them? Or: do you hear them and yet not take heed from them? The reproach in the first reading is directed at both the failure to hear and the failure to take heed together, and in the second reading at the failure to take heed while the thing that necessitates it, namely hearing, is actually realized.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 32, verse 5 (part 1 of 2):

﴿He arranges the affair﴾. It is said: that is, the affair of this world and its circumstances. The origin of tadbir (arrangement, management) is looking into the outcome of a matter and reflecting on it so that it comes out with a praiseworthy end. With regard to Him, glorified and exalted, it is a metaphor for willing a thing in a manner of perfection (itqan) and with regard to wisdom (hikmah). The verb is implicitly understood to carry the meaning of sending down (inzal), and the two prepositional phrases in His words, ﴿from the heaven to the earth﴾, are attached to it. "Min" (from) indicates the starting point, and "ila" (to) indicates the endpoint. That is, He, exalted be He, wills it in a manner of perfection and with regard to wisdom, sending it down from the heaven to the earth. Its descent from the heaven is in terms of its causes, for its causes are heavenly, from the angels, peace be upon them, and others. ﴿Then it ascends﴾: that is, that affair rises and ascends to Him, glorified and exalted, after its arrangement. This ascent is a metaphor for its being established in His knowledge, exalted be He; that is, His knowledge, glorified be He, becomes related to it in an actual manner, by His knowing it as existing in fact. Or it is a metaphor for its being written in the scrolls of the angels, peace be upon them, who are charged with His command, glorified and exalted, as existing in that way. ﴿In a day whose measure is a thousand years of what you count﴾: that is, in an extended span of time. The intended meaning is not the literal number. The extended period is expressed by the thousand because it is the furthest of the levels and the ultimate of the limits, and there is no level above it except what branches from it among the numbers of its levels. The two verbs are in a relation of contention (tanazu') regarding the prepositional phrase and the noun it governs, and the second of them has been made to govern it. So the verse indicates the great length of time between the attachment of His will, glorified be He, to the existence of events at their appointed times, arranged with perfection and with regard to wisdom, and their existence in that manner. Its apparent sense requires that their existence does not depend on the attachment of the will a second time, but that the earlier attachment suffices for it. It is also said: "in a day" is attached to "ya'ruju" (ascends), and the two verbs are not in contention regarding it. The meaning of the affair's ascent to Him after His arrangement of it, glorified be He, is the arrival of the news of its existence in fact, just as it was arranged through the angel, and its presentation in a presence that He, exalted be His majesty, has prepared for testing, by what He knows best, to manifest the perfection of His greatness, blessed and exalted be He, and the magnitude of His sovereignty, may His sovereignty be exalted. This is like the presentation of the deeds of the servants to the angels, peace be upon them, which is mentioned in the reports. And "a thousand years" is in its literal sense, and it is the distance between the earth and the convex of the lower heaven by the ordinary pace of humans, for the distance between the heaven and the earth is five hundred years, and the thickness of the heaven is likewise, as came in the sound reports, while the angel covers that in a short time. So the speech is by way of comparison. It is as if it were said: He wills the affair perfected and with regard to wisdom, by heavenly causes whose effects and rulings descend to the earth, so it comes to be as He willed, glorified be He. Then that affair ascends with the angel, and its news rises to His presence, glorified be He, in a time that is like a thousand years of what you count. It is also said: the ascent to Him, exalted be He, is the ascent of the news of the affair with the angel to Him, glorified and exalted, as is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah and al-Dahhak. The two verbs are in contention regarding "day," and the intended meaning is that it is the time of arranging the affair, if humans were to arrange it, and the time of ascent if they were also to ascend, [and] otherwise the time of arrangement and ascent is short. It is also said: the meaning is: He arranges the affair of the world by manifesting it in the Preserved Tablet, so the angel charged with it descends from the heaven to the earth, then the angel, or the affair with the angel, returns to Him, exalted be He, in a time which, regarding the descent and ascent, is like a thousand years of what you count. By it is intended the measure of what lies between the earth and the concave of the lower heaven, going and returning. The apparent sense is that "He arranges" is implicitly carrying the meaning of sending down, and the two prepositional phrases are attached to it, not to an omitted verb, meaning that the angel descends with it from the heaven to the earth as has been said. Some have claimed that the pronoun in "ilayhi" refers to the heaven, which is sometimes feminine-marked, as in His words: ﴿the heaven will be split asunder by it﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 18]. It is also said: the meaning is that He, glorified be He, arranges the affair of the whole world from the heaven to the earth for every day of the days of the Lord, glorified be His state, and that is a thousand years, as He, glorified be He, said: ﴿Indeed, a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count﴾ [al-Hajj: 47]. Then it comes back to Him, exalted be He, is established with Him, glorified and exalted be He, and He writes in the scrolls of His angels, exalted and glorified be He, every moment of the moments of this period, of what ascends from that affair, and enters into existence until the period reaches its end. Then He arranges again for another day, and so on, until the Hour is established. This is pointed to by what is related from Mujahid, who said: He, exalted be He, arranges and casts to the angels the affairs of a thousand years of our years, and that is a day in His presence, exalted be He. When it is finished, He casts to them the like of it. In this case "the affair" means the matter or business, and the two prepositional phrases are attached to it, or to an omitted circumstantial element (hal) of it. There is no implicit meaning in "yudabbiru." The ascent to Him, exalted be He, is a metaphor for its establishment and its being written in the scrolls of the angels. "A thousand years" is in its literal sense. "In a day" is attached to both verbs, and the second has been made to govern it, as if it were said: He arranges the affair for a day whose measure is such-and-such, then it ascends to Him, exalted be He, in it, just as you say: "I intended and looked into the book," meaning: I intended toward the book and looked into it. The difference of the two complements does not prevent contention. The recurrence of arrangement until the Day of Resurrection is indicated by the shift to the present tense, although the affair is past, as if it were said: He renews this affair continuously. It is also said: the meaning is: He arranges the affair of the world from the heaven to the earth until the Hour is established. Then that whole affair ascends to Him, exalted be He, that is, it goes to Him, glorified be He, that He may judge in it in a day whose measure is a thousand years, and that is the Day of Resurrection. In this case "the affair" means the matter, and the two prepositional phrases are attached to it, or to an omitted circumstantial element of it, as in the preceding view. The ascent to Him, exalted be He, is the going to Him, glorified be He, not for it to be recorded in the scrolls of the angels, but for Him, exalted be He, to judge in it.

(In a day) is attached to the ascent, and there is no contention. The day whose measure is such-and-such is the Day of Resurrection. This does not contradict His words, exalted be He: ﴿whose measure is fifty thousand years﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 4], on one of the two interpretations of it, due to the variation in the perceived length according to the intensity [of the situation], or because there are fifty stations, each station being a thousand years. It is also said: the meaning is: the revelation descends with Gabriel, peace be upon him, from the heaven to the earth, then what was accepted of it, or rejected, returns to Him, exalted be He, with Gabriel, peace be upon him, in a day whose measure of travel is a thousand years, which is the distance between the heaven and the earth, going down and coming up. So "the affair" in this view means the revelation, as in His words: ﴿He casts the Spirit by His command﴾ [Ghafir: 15]. The ascent to Him, exalted be He, is an expression for the news of acceptance and rejection, with Gabriel, peace be upon him, ascending. The arrangement and the ascent are in the day, but in an extended and distributed sense. So the two verbs are in contention regarding the adverbial phrase, but there is no difference in the complement. On this view, the verse is not contradicted by His words, glorified be His affair: ﴿The angels and the Spirit ascend to Him in a day whose measure is fifty thousand years﴾, on the other interpretation of it, which you will come to know, God willing, because the ascent there is to the Throne, while here it is to the lower heaven, and both are an ascent to God, exalted be He, by way of figurative extension.

It is also said: the intended meaning of "the affair" is the commanded matter, of acts of obedience and righteous deeds. The meaning is: He, glorified be He, sends that down arranged from the heaven to the earth, then it is not acted upon, and that commanded matter does not ascend to Him, exalted be He, sincere and pleasing to Him, except after a long period, because of the scarcity of the sincere among the servants. On this view "He arranges" implicitly carries the meaning of sending down, and "from" and "to" are attached to it. The meaning of ascent is rising, as in His words, exalted be He: ﴿To Him ascends the good word﴾ [Fatir: 10]. The purpose of the alif (the thousand) is to express the length of the period. The meaning is the rarity of the worship of the sincere, and the length of the period between the arrangement and its occurrence. "Thumma" (then) is for remoteness, and this meaning is supported by His words that follow it: ﴿little is it that you give thanks﴾ [al-A'raf: 10; al-Mu'minun: 78; al-Sajdah: 9], because the speech is connected, part to part, and the scarcity of thanks despite those blessings indicates the rarity mentioned.

It is also said: the meaning is: He arranges the affairs of the sun in its rising from the east and its setting in the west, and its course in the world from the heaven to the earth, and the time from its rising until it sets and returns to its place of rising, its distance being a thousand years, and it covers that in a day and a night. This is what they have said about the noble verse in explaining its intended meaning. It is not hidden from anyone of understanding how forced most of these sayings are, and how very contrary to the apparent sense. They are before you, so choose for yourself what pleases you. It appears to me that by "the heaven" is meant the direction of height, like its usage in His words: ﴿Are you secure from He who is in the heaven?﴾ [al-Mulk: 16]. By the ascent of the affair to Him, exalted be He, is meant the ascent of its news, as has been heard from the group. "In a day" is attached to the ascent without contention. I say: this verse is among the ambiguous (mutashabih) verses, and I hold that God, exalted be He, arranges the affairs and circumstances of the world and wills them perfected, and He, glorified be He, is established upon His Throne, and that is the arrangement from the direction of height. Then the news of that ascends with the angel to Him, glorified and exalted be He, to manifest the increase of His greatness, may His greatness be exalted, and the magnitude of His sovereignty, may His sovereignty be magnified, for wisdoms that He, exalted be He, knows best. All of this is with a meaning fitting for Him, exalted be He, combining transcendence (tanzih) and distinct from anthropomorphism (tashbih), as the early scholars (salaf) say concerning such things. The saying of some of them: "The Throne is the place of arrangement, what is below it is the place of detail, and what is below the heavens is the place of disposal," contains a scent of what we have mentioned. As for the estimation of the day of ascent here as a thousand years, and in another verse as fifty thousand years, much has been said about its explanation, and some of it has preceded for you.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn al-Anbari in al-Masahif, and al-Hakim, who declared it sound, related from 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Mulaykah, who said: I and 'Abd Allah ibn Fayruz, freedman of 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, may Allah be pleased with him, entered upon Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, and he asked him about the words of God, exalted be He: ﴿He arranges the affair from the heaven to the earth, then it ascends to Him in a day whose measure is a thousand years﴾. Ibn 'Abbas seemed to suspect him, and said: What is a day whose measure is fifty thousand years? He said: I only asked you so that you would inform me. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: They are two days which Allah mentioned in His Book; Allah knows best about them, and I dislike saying in the Book of Allah what I do not know. Time passed through its vicissitudes until I sat with Ibn al-Musayyib, and a man asked him about them, but he did not inform him and did not know. I said: Shall I not inform you of what I heard from Ibn 'Abbas? He said: Yes. So I informed him, and he said to the questioner: This is Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, who refused to speak about them, and he knows more than I do.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 32, verse 5 (part 2 of 2):

Some of the Sufis (mutasawwifa) call the day measured as a thousand years the "Lordly Day" (al-yawm al-rububi), and the day measured as fifty thousand years the "Divine Day" (al-yawm al-ilahi). Muhyi al-Din (may his secret be sanctified) calls the first "the Day of the Lord" (yawm al-Rabb) and the second "the Day of the Ascensions" (yawm al-ma'arij), and he mentioned that, along with other days, such as the Day of Affair (yawm al-sha'n), the Day of the Likeness (yawm al-mithl), the Day of the Moon (yawm al-qamar), the Day of the Sun (yawm al-shams), the Day of Saturn (yawm Zuhal), the days of the rest of the planets (sayyara), the Day of Aries (yawm al-hamal), and the days of the rest of the zodiacal signs (burj), in al-Futuhat (al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya).

I asked the head of the unveiling-based sect (al-ta'ifa al-kashfiyya) that has emerged in our age, in Karbala, about a question, and he wrote what he wrote in answering it, and he digressed into explaining the usages of the word "day" (yawm). He counted from that sixty-four usages, among them its use for the Lordly Day and its use for the Divine Day, and he extended his discourse on that topic. Perhaps, God willing, we will transmit to you from it something substantial in another place. God willing, we will also mention the complete discussion concerning the reconciliation of this verse with His words, glorified is He: ﴿The angels and the Spirit ascend to Him in a day whose measure is fifty thousand years﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 4]. And His words, exalted is He: ﴿of what you count﴾ is an attribute of "a thousand" (alfa), or an attribute of "year" (sana).

Ibn Abi Ablah read "yu'raju" in the passive voice, and the original is "yu'raju bihi," so the preposition was dropped and the pronoun became implicit. Jannah ibn Hubaysh read "thumma ya'ruju al-malaikatu" ilayhi with the addition of "al-malaika." Abu Hayyan said: "Perhaps it is an explanation from him of its having fallen out of the body of the Mushaf."

al-Sulami, Ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, and al-Hasan (with a variant reported from him) read "ya'udduna" with the yā' of the third person.

﴿That﴾, i.e., the Essence described by those attributes that necessitate complete power and all-encompassing wisdom, ﴿Knower of the unseen﴾, i.e., of everything hidden from creation, ﴿and the witnessed﴾, i.e., of everything creation witnesses. He, glory be to Him, manages all of that in accordance with wisdom. It has been said: the unseen is the Hereafter and the witnessed is this world. ﴿the Mighty﴾, the one who prevails over His affair, ﴿the Merciful﴾ toward His servants. In this there is an indication that He, mighty and majestic, acts with grace in what He does, exalted is He. The demonstrative ﴿that﴾ is a *mubtada'* (subject of a nominal sentence), and the three attributes after it are *akhbar* (predicates) of it. It is also permissible for the first to be the *khabar* (predicate), and the last two to be *na't* (qualifiers) of the first.

Zayd ibn ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with both of them, read the three attributes in the genitive (*khafd*), on the basis that ﴿that﴾ refers to the affair, which is in the nominative position as the *fa'il* (agent) of the verb *yaʿruju* (ascends). The attributes are in the genitive as a *badal* (substitute, or apposition) of the pronoun in *ilayhi* (to Him). Abu Zayd al-Nahwi read the last two attributes in the genitive, on the basis that ﴿that﴾ refers to Allah, exalted is He, and is in the nominative position as a *mubtada'*, with *ʿalimu* (knower) as its *khabar*, and the two attributes are in the genitive as a *badal* of the pronoun.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 32, verse 7:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Who made everything He created good﴾ is a fourth predicate (khabar) or a third attribute (na't), or it is in the accusative on the basis of praise (nusiba 'ala al-madh). Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be the predicate of an elided subject (mubtada' mahdhuf), meaning "He is the One who," and that al-'Aziz is the subject (mubtada'), al-Rahim is its attribute (sifa), and this is its predicate; and that the clause ﴿khalaqahu﴾ (He created it) is in the genitive position as an attribute of "shay'" (thing). It is also permissible that it be in the accusative position as an attribute of "kull" (everything). The possibility of it being a fresh sentence (isti'naf) is remote. The meaning is that He, glorified is He, made every one of His created things good, because there is not one thing among them except that it is arranged according to what wisdom requires and what the interest demands. Thus all created things are good, even though they differ in degrees of goodness, as His saying, exalted is He, indicates: ﴿We have certainly created man in the best of stature﴾ [al-Tin: 4]. He negated disparity in His creation, exalted is He, in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿You will not see in the creation of the Most Merciful any inconsistency﴾ [al-Mulk: 3], in a sense that you will come to know, God willing, which does not contradict what has been mentioned. It has also been permitted that the meaning is: He knew how to create it, from the saying "the worth of a man is what he does well" (qimat al-mar'i ma yuhsinu); its real sense is "he does well in knowing it," i.e., he knows it with a good knowledge, with verification and certainty. Its remoteness is not hidden.

Al-'Arabiyyan (Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i, in the sense of the two Arab readers) and Ibn Kathir read ﴿khalqahu﴾ with a sukun on the lam. It has been said that it is a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal) from "kull," and the pronoun attached to it refers back to it, and it remains on the verbal-noun (masdar) meaning. It has also been said that it is a substitution of the whole from the whole (badal kull min kull), or a substitution of part from the whole (badal ba'd min kull), with the pronoun referring to God, exalted is He, and it has the meaning of the created thing (makhluq). It has also been said that it is a second object (maf'ul thani) of "ahsana," with it being made to imply the meaning of "a'ta" (gave), meaning: He, glorified is He, gave every thing its creation suited to it by way of beneficence and grace. It has also been said that it is the first object, with "kull shay'" as the second object, and its pronoun refers to God, glorified is He, with "ihsan" being made to imply the meaning of "ilham" (inspiration), as al-Farra' said, or "ta'rif" (making known), as Abu al-Baqa' said. The meaning is: He inspired, or made known, His creation with everything that they need, and this returns to the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Who gave everything its creation, then guided it﴾ [Ta-Ha: 50].

Abu 'Ali, in al-Hujja, preferred what Sibawayh mentioned in al-Kitab, that it is an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) of "ahsana" from its meaning, and the pronoun refers to God, exalted is He, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The handiwork of God﴾ [al-Naml: 88], ﴿the promise of God﴾ [al-Nisa': 122 and elsewhere], and ﴿And He began the creation of man﴾, meaning Adam, peace be upon him, ﴿from clay﴾. Or [it means] He began the creation of this known species ﴿from clay﴾, where He began the creation of Adam, peace be upon him, as a creation containing within it the innate nature of all the individuals of the species, in a general, summary containment.

Al-Zuhri read "bada" with an alif in place of the hamzah. He said in al-Bahr:

The analogy for "hada'a" (to be at ease) and "hada" is not the substitution of the hamzah with an alif; rather the analogy for this hamzah is facilitation (tas-hil) between-between (bayn bayn). Moreover, al-Akhfash related "qara'tu" as "qaraytu." It has been said that this is the dialect of the Ansar: they say in "bada'a," "badiya," with a kasra on the middle radical of the root and a ya' after it. And the tribe of Ta'i say, for verbs like this, "baqiya" as "baqa," like "rama." So it is possible that al-Zuhri's reading is in accordance with this dialect, with the original being "badiya," then it became "bada." And in the dialect of the Ansar, Ibn Rawaha said:

By the name of God and in Him we began, and had we worshipped other than Him we would have been wretched.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 32, verse 8:

﴿Then He made his offspring⦗nasl⦘﴾ i.e., his progeny (dhurriyyah). They were called nasl because they are drawn out (tansallu) and separated from him, ﴿from an extract⦗sulalah⦘﴾ i.e., an essence, whose root meaning is that which is drawn out and extracted by refining, ﴿from a fluid of despised⦗maheen⦘ water﴾, meaning one that is treated with contempt and not cared for, and it is the seminal fluid (al-maniyy).

Al-Alusi, Ruh al-Ma'ani, on Surah 32, verse 9:

﴿Then He proportioned him﴾: He made him balanced (muʿaddalahu) by perfecting his limbs in the womb and shaping them as they should be. The root of taswiyah (proportioning, equalizing) is making the parts equal. (Thumma) here indicates sequence, either in rank (al-tartib al-rutbi) or in mention (al-tartib al-dhikri).

﴿And breathed into him of His spirit﴾: He attributed the spirit (ruh) to Himself, exalting it, as in "the House of Allah" and "the she-camel of Allah." It also signals that it is a wondrous creation and a marvelous making. It was said that He attributed it to Himself to hint that it has a certain station connected to the presence of Lordship (hadrat al-rububiyyah).

From here Abu Bakr al-Razi said: "Whoever knows himself knows his Lord." As for the breathing of the spirit, it was said that it is a metaphor for making it attached to the body. This is more in accord with the view of those who hold that the spirit is immaterial and not located within the body, among the philosophers and some of the theologians, such as Hujjat al-Islam al-Ghazali, may Allah have mercy on him. It was also said that it is literal, and the one who directly does it is the angel appointed over the womb. To this view went those who hold that the spirit is a subtle body like air, which pervades the body as rose-water pervades the rose and fire pervades the ember, and this is what the apparent meanings of the reports support. The scholar Ibn al-Qayyim established about a hundred proofs for it.

﴿And made for you hearing, sight, and hearts﴾: This is a shift to address (iltifat ila al-khitab). The placement of its mention after the breathing of the spirit is clear, and its honoring with the robe of address when it became fit for address. The making (jaʿl) is creative (ibda'i), and the preposition (lam) is connected to it. The fronting of the direct object is, as has been repeatedly noted, for emphasis on what is fronted and to create anticipation for what is delayed, along with the fact that it is lengthy, which fronting it would disrupt the eloquence of the noble arrangement. The hearing is fronted because of the abundance of its benefits, for most matters of religion are known only through it. It is given in singular because it is originally a verbal noun (masdar).

It was also said: this is to hint that its perceiver is one kind, namely sound, unlike sight, which perceives light, color, shape, motion and stillness, and unlike the heart, which perceives the objects of the senses through them. And in addition to that, i.e., He created those faculties for your benefit so that you would know that they, while in themselves being great blessings whose worth cannot be measured, are means to enjoying all the other religious and worldly blessings poured upon you, and that you would thank Him by directing each of them to what it was created for: you perceive with your hearing the revealed signs that declare tawhid and resurrection, with your sight the created signs that witness to them, and with your hearts you derive proof of their truth.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Little is it that you give thanks﴾ is an explanation of their ingratitude for those blessings by way of an interjected concluding remark (i'tiradh tadhyili). The word "little" (qillah) carries the sense of negation, as what follows indicates.

The adjective is in the accusative as an attribute of an omitted noun that functions as the object of "you give thanks" (li-tashkurun), meaning: "a little thanks you give," or "for a little time you give thanks."

Al-Khafaji, may Allah have mercy on him, preferred that the sentence be a circumstantial clause (haliyyah) rather than an interjected one (i'tiradiyyah).

**[Page 125]**

*"They say"* (﴿وقالوا﴾): this is a new sentence, introduced to expose their falsehoods by way of *iltifat* (a shift in grammatical person, from address to third-person narration). This signals that their failure to be grateful for those blessings warrants turning away from them, and that listing their crimes against others is done in a manner of *mubathah* (a polite, indirect manner of speech that, in this context, is akin to a jest). It is narrated that the speaker was Ubayy ibn Khalaf, and the plural pronoun is used because the rest approved of his words. Their words are: ﴿Is it that when we have gone astray in the earth﴾, meaning: were lost in it, by becoming dust mixed with its dust so that we cannot be distinguished from it, from *dalla al-mata'u* (the goods were lost) when they are misplaced; or we became hidden in it by burial, even if we do not become dust. Qutrub adopted this interpretation and cited the verse of al-Nabighah lamenting al-Nu'man ibn al-Mundhir:

*"His slayers returned with a clear sign,*
*and Hazm and Na'il were left behind at al-Jawlan."*

Yahya ibn Ya'mar, Ibn Muhaysin, Abu Raja', Talhah and Ibn Wathhab read *ḍalilnā* (ضَلِلْنا) with a kasrah on the lam. It is said that *ḍalla yaḍillu* is like *ḍaraba yaḍribu*, and *ḍalla yaḍillu* is like *ʿalima yaʿlamu*; both have the same meaning. The first is the well-known and eloquent dialect, the dialect of Najd, while the second is the dialect of the people of al-ʿĀliyah. Abu Haywah read *ḍulilnā* (ضُلِلْنا) with a ḍammah on the ḍād and a kasrah on the lam; this reading is also reported from ʿAli, may Allah ennoble his face.

Al-Hasan, al-A'mash and Aban ibn Sa'id ibn al-As read *ṣalalnā* (صَلَلْنا) with an unmarked ṣād and a fatḥah on the lam. This is attributed to ʿAli, may Allah ennoble his face, to Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and to al-Hasan, who is also reported to have read it with a kasrah on the lam. It is said of it what is said of *ḍalla* with the marked ḍād, and also *aṣalla* with a hamzah, as in the pattern *afʿala*. Al-Farra' said: the meaning is "we became *al-ṣilah*," which is dry, hard earth, as if it were named from *al-ṣalīl* (a ringing sound), because dry, hard ground makes a ringing sound when it cracks. It is also said: "we became putrid," from *al-ṣilah*, which means stench; and the earth is called *al-ṣilah* because it is the anus of the world. The Arabs say: "Put the *ṣilah* upon the *ṣilah*." Al-Nahhas said: "We do not know *ṣalalnā* in the language; but it is said *aṣalla al-laḥmu* and *ṣalla*, and *akhamma* and *khamma*, when it stinks." This is a strange remark from him.

Ibn ʿAmir read *idhā* (إذا) without the interrogative particle, and the intended meaning is an assertion in the manner of mockery and derision. The governing element of *idhā* is what is indicated by the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Are we indeed in a new creation?﴾ (﴿أإنا لفي خلق جديد﴾), namely *nubʿathu* (we shall be resurrected) or *yujaddadu khalquna* (our creation shall be renewed). The verb cannot be the governing element itself because of the presence of the interrogative; and even if the two are considered together, the element after them does not govern what precedes it. What was mentioned, *nubʿathu* or *yujaddadu khalquna*, is considered the answer to *idhā*, if *idhā* is treated as conditional and not as purely temporal. The hamzah is for denial, and the intent is to emphasize the denial, not to deny the emphasis, as is apparent from placing it before its particle, although it is posterior to it in meaning; its placement before it is due to the strength of its requirement to stand at the head of the sentence.

Nafiʿ, al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read *innā* (إنا) without the interrogative particle, in the manner mentioned above. ﴿Nay, they are disbelievers in the meeting with their Lord﴾ (﴿بل هم بلقاء ربهم كافرون﴾): this is a change of direction (*idrab*, a turning away) and a transition from explaining their disbelief in the resurrection to explaining something more emphatic and more shocking, namely their disbelief in the meeting with the angels of their Lord at the time of death and everything that follows it. It has also been said that it is a change of direction and an escalation, from hesitation about the resurrection and deeming it unlikely, to a definite denial of it, on the basis that the meeting with the Lord is a metaphor for the resurrection. According to al-Khafaji, the fact that the preceding interrogative is a denial, which ultimately amounts to a rejection, does not prevent this reading. So reflect on this.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 32, verse 11:

﴿Say﴾, in rejection of them, ﴿The Angel of Death who has been entrusted with you will take you (yatawaffakum)﴾, he will complete (yastawfi) your souls, leaving nothing of their parts behind, or he will leave nothing of their particulars behind, and he will not leave any one of you alive. The root of tawaffi (taking in full) is the taking of a thing in its entirety, and it has been explained as istifa' (complete taking), because tafa''ala and istif'āla often coincide, as in taqaḍḍaytuhu and istaqḍaytuhu, and ta'ajjaltuhu and isti'jaltuhu. The attribution of tawaffi to the Angel of Death is on the basis that he, peace be upon him, directly seizes souls by the command of Him, mighty and majestic, as alluded to in the saying of Him, glorified be He: ﴿who has been entrusted with you﴾, that is, with taking your souls and knowing the ends of your terms.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ entered upon a man of the Ansar to visit him, and there was the Angel of Death, peace be upon him, at his head. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: (O Angel of Death, be gentle with my companion, for he is a believer). He said: Rejoice, O Muhammad, for I am gentle with every believer. And know, O Muhammad, that I seize the soul of the son of Adam and his family cries out, so I stand in a corner of the house and say: By Allah, I have no sin. Indeed, there is a returning and a returning. Beware, beware. Allah the Exalted has not created any household, nor clay, nor hair, nor wool, on land or sea, except that I inspect them every day and night five times, until I know their young and their old better than they know themselves. By Allah, O Muhammad, I cannot seize the soul of a gnat until Allah, blessed and exalted, is the One who commands its seizure.)" Al-Tabarani, Abu Nu'aym and Ibn Mandah narrated something similar.

Its attribution to Him, mighty and majestic, in the saying of Him, glorified be He: ﴿Allah takes the souls﴾ [al-Zumar: 42] is on the basis that all the actions of the servants are created by Him, exalted be He, and the servants have no part in them beyond acquisition (kasb), as the Ash'aris say; or on the basis that this occurs by His permission and will, exalted is His majesty. Its attribution to the messengers in the saying of Him, exalted be He: ﴿Our messengers take him (tawaffathu rusulunā)﴾ [al-An'am: 61], and to the angels in the saying of Him, glorified be He: ﴿Those whom the angels take (tatawaffāhumu al-malā'ikatu) while they are wronging themselves﴾ [al-Nahl: 28], is because the Angel of Death does not act alone; rather he has assistants, as is reported in the traditions, who labour at drawing out the soul until, when its departure draws near, the Angel of Death seizes it. It has been said that by "the Angel of Death" is meant the category (al-jins). Some have said that the Angel of Death takes some people, and Allah, mighty and majestic, takes others Himself.

Ibn Majah narrated from Abu Umamah, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: 'Allah, exalted be He, has entrusted the Angel of Death, peace be upon him, with seizing the spirits, except the martyrs of the sea, for He, glorified be He, Himself takes charge of seizing their spirits.'"

This is also found in another report indicating that the Angel of Death for humans is other than the Angel of Death for jinn, devils, and what does not reason.

Ibn Juwayr narrated from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: The Angel of Death, peace be upon him, was entrusted with seizing the spirits of the believers; he is the one who directly undertakes seizing their spirits. There is an angel over the jinn, an angel over the devils, and an angel over birds, beasts, predators, fish and ants; thus they are four angels. The angels die at the first blast, and the Angel of Death directly undertakes seizing their spirits and then dies. As for the martyrs at sea, Allah, exalted be He, directly undertakes seizing their spirits and does not entrust that to the Angel of Death, out of honour for them before Him, glorified be He.

What the majority hold is that the Angel of Death is one for those who reason and for those among animals who do not reason, and he is 'Azrail, whose meaning is said to be "the servant of Allah." Yet, as we have mentioned, he has assistants. As for the report of al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas, Allah knows best its soundness. ﴿Then to your Lord you will be returned﴾ for resurrection, for reckoning and recompense. The connection of this verse with what precedes it, according to what we mentioned regarding the explanation of the transition (al-iḍrāb), is evident: for when they denied meeting the angels of their Lord at death and what follows it, He mentioned to them the account of the Angel of Death's taking them, as a hint that they would meet him, and the account of the return to Allah, exalted be He, for resurrection, reckoning and recompense. As for what has been said, the connection is that when they denied resurrection and return, He answered them with what He mentioned, since the saying of Him, exalted be He: ﴿Then to your Lord you will be returned﴾ includes resurrection and more; He mentioned the Angel of Death's taking them and his being entrusted with them, because the resurrection depends on their death, and as a threat and warning, and to indicate that the One able to cause death is able to bring to life. It has also been said that this is to refute what their speech implies, that death is by the demand of nature, since they attributed it to themselves in their saying: ﴿When we have gone astray in the earth﴾; so it is not, in their view, by the act of Allah exalted be He and the working of His angels. Its remoteness is not hidden. Even more remote is what has been said regarding the connection: that 'Azrail, who is one of His servants, when he is able to separate the spirit from the body while it permeates it like rose-water permeates the rose and fire permeates the ember, how then would the Creator of powers and capacities, exalted is His majesty, be unable to distinguish their parts mixed with the dust? How would resurrection be deemed unlikely with His complete power, mighty and majestic, since that permeation is among the things hidden from the intelligent, to the point that some of them denied it, so how of the ignorant polytheists? So reflect. Zayd ibn 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, read "turja'ūn" (you are returned) in the active voice.

[p. 127]

﴿And if you could see when the criminals﴾, namely those who say: ﴿"Shall we, when we have gone astray in the earth..."﴾, or the category of criminals, of whom they are a part, ﴿hanging their heads﴾, bowing them in shame and humiliation, ﴿before their Lord﴾ at the time of their reckoning, when there has not appeared from their ugly deeds, which they committed in the world, what has appeared. Zayd ibn 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with them both) read «nakkasū ru'ūsahum» as a past-tense verb with an object. ﴿Our Lord﴾ is then governed by an implied verb of saying in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and the governing element of that clause is (nākisū, "hanging"), meaning: they say, "Our Lord, etc." This is preferable to the estimate that they are calling for help by their saying, "Our Lord."

[p. 127 continues]

﴿We have seen and heard﴾, meaning: we have become among those who see and hear, and we have attained the readiness to perceive the seeing signs and the heard signs; previously we were blind and deaf, perceiving nothing. ﴿So return us﴾ to the world ﴿that we may do righteous deeds﴾ in accordance with what those signs require. This, as has been said, is a claim on their part to the soundness of the faculties of sight and hearing. The statement of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿Indeed we are certain﴾, is a resumptive sentence (isti'nāf) explaining what precedes it. It has been said that it is a resumptive sentence not intended as a causal explanation (ta'līl). On both estimates, it implies their claim to the soundness of the hearts and their capacity to understand the meanings of the signs and to act in accordance with what they require. It also contains a display of steadfastness in certainty and the completeness of their desire for it, and perhaps for this reason they did not say, "We have seen, heard, and become certain, so return us," etc. The reason the hearing is placed after the seeing may be that most of the promised righteous deeds result from hearing and not from sight, so it was preferable not to separate the two with sight. It is also permissible to posit for each of the two verbs an object appropriate to it, from among what they see and hear, such that it is said: "We have seen the resurrection which we used to deny, and what You promised us in return for denying it, and we have heard from You what indicates the truthfulness of Your messengers, peace be upon them." This is intended to mean something like Allah's saying: ﴿O assembly of jinn and humankind, did there not come to you messengers from among you, relating to you My signs and warning you of the meeting of this your day?﴾ [al-An'ām 6:130], not an explicit report in the words "that My messengers are truthful," for example. Or it may be said: "We have seen the resurrection and what You promised us, and we have heard the words of the messengers," meaning we heard them with the hearing of obedience and submission. Or it may be said: "We have seen the ugliness of our deeds, which we used to see as good in the world, and we have heard the words of the angels to us: indeed your return is to the Fire." It has also been said: they meant, "We saw Your messengers and heard their speech when we were in the world," or "We saw Your created signs and heard Your revealed signs in the world, so the proof is yours against us, and we have no proof; so return us," etc. The condition of this view is not hidden. On all these estimates, the reason for placing sight before hearing is clear. The particle «law» (lau), which many have called imtinā'iyya (expressing the impossibility of the consequent), has its consequent omitted, the estimate being: "you would have seen a dreadful matter whose extent cannot be measured."

[p. 128]

The address in «tarā» (you see) is to everyone who is capable of seeing, since the purpose is to explain the completeness of their evil condition and how far it has reached in dreadfulness, to the point that its strangeness and terribleness is not restricted to one who sees over another who sees, from among those accustomed to witnessing wondrous matters and grave calamities; rather, everyone who is capable of seeing is amazed at its horror and dreadfulness. It has also been said that this is because the aim is to show that their state has reached such manifestness that its concealment is absolutely impossible, so its sight is not restricted to one viewer over another. The omitted consequent is more suitable to what was mentioned first. The verb is treated as intransitive, so no object is estimated for it, meaning: if you were to have sight at that time, you would see a dreadful matter. It is also permitted that the address be specific to the master of those addressed, ﷺ, and «law» may then be for expressing a wish (tamannī), as if it were said: "Would that you could see when the criminals hang their heads, so that you might gloat over them." The ruling on a wish from Him, the Exalted, is the ruling on hope (tarajjī), which has been discussed earlier, and according to the majority there is then no consequent for it. Abū Ḥayyān and Ibn Mālik said that it must have a consequent, citing the verse of Muhalhil in the War of al-Basūs:

"If the graves were dug up for Kulayb, so that he might inform about the Dhanā'ib what kind of stalk (ziyr) he was,
on the day of al-Sha'tamayn, his eye would be delighted; but how can there be a meeting with one who is under the graves?"

Here «law» (if only) is for a wish, as shown by the accusative «fa-yukhbira» (so that he might inform), and it has a consequent, namely «la-qarra» (his eye would be delighted). It was objected that it is conditional, and that «fa-yukhbira» is a conjunction upon a verbal noun (maṣdar) inferred from «nubisha» (was dug up), as if it were said: "If there were a digging up, then an informing," and what this involves of artificiality is not hidden. Al-Khafājī, may Allah have mercy on him, said: it might be said that «law» for the estimate of a wish, when it is frequently accompanied by it, is given its ruling, and it is dispensed with estimating a consequent for it when none is mentioned, as in the conjunctive use (waṣliyya); and the accusative of its consequent would have been easier than what was mentioned. It is also permitted that an object be estimated for «tarā» (you see), indicated by what follows it, meaning: "if you saw the criminals," or "if you saw their hanging their heads." The past tense is used with «law» (in its imtinā'iyya sense) and «idh» (when) because His, the Exalted's, report of what is established in His eternal knowledge, given its certainty, is like the past, so what indicates the past is used for it metaphorically (majāz), as with «law» and «idh». This. Among the strange things is the statement of Abū al-'Abbās concerning the verse: the meaning is: "Say, O Muhammad, to the criminal, 'If you could see...'" Abū Ḥayyān related this from him and then said: he considered that the sentence is conjoined to («yatawaffākum», "takes you back") and falls under the earlier («qul», "say"); that is why the address in it was not made to the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace. End of his statement. So do not be heedless.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 32, verse 13:

﴿And if We had willed, We would have given every soul its guidance﴾ is governed by a supposed statement, conjoined to a supposed statement before His words, the Exalted: ﴿Our Lord, we have seen and heard﴾, and so on. It is the answer to their saying ﴿So send us back﴾. It indicates that if they were sent back they would return to what they had been forbidden, because of their evil choice, and that they are among those to whom God, the Exalted, has not willed to give guidance. That is, [it means]: "And We say: if We had willed," that is, if Our will had been related in an active manner to giving every soul, both the pious and the wicked, its guidance, that is, that by which it would be guided to faith and righteous action. Some of them explained it as faith itself and righteous action, but the first [explanation] is preferable. As for explaining it as what the many asked for, namely return to the world, or as guidance to Paradise, this is nothing [of substance]. We would have given it to them in this world, which is the abode of earning, and We did not postpone it to the abode of recompense. ﴿But the word from Me has come true﴾, that is, My word was established and confirmed, and My decree had preceded, when I said to Iblis, at his saying: ﴿I will surely mislead them all﴾ ﴿except Your sincere servants among them﴾, and ﴿So the truth is, and the truth I say: I will surely fill Hell with you and with those who follow you among them, all together﴾ [Sad: 84, 85]. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿I will surely fill Hell with jinn and men, all together﴾, as is indicated by the placing of the jinn before the men, for in the address to Iblis it is placed first; and its placement there is because it is more fitting to the station of belittling that addressee, upon whom be the curse. It has been said that the placement in both places is because the jinn destined for Hell are more numerous.

From what we have mentioned, the reason for the shift from the pronoun of majesty in His words, glorified is He: ﴿And if We had willed, We would have given﴾ to the pronoun of singularity in His words, exalted is He: ﴿But the word from Me has come true﴾ becomes clear. This is because what was mentioned refers to what occurred in the reply to the accursed one, and in it the saying and the filling were attributed to the pronoun of singularity, so that the discourse would be in the style of ﴿I will surely mislead them all﴾ ﴿except Your servants﴾ [Sad: 82, 83] in the unification of the pronoun. It may also be said: the pronoun of majesty is more suited to the multiplicity indicated by ﴿every soul﴾, while the other pronoun is more suited to what is less than that multiplicity, indicated by (from the jinn and men). Or it may be said that He made the pronoun singular in the threat because the one intended is the polytheists; it is as if He placed the discourse in a way in which no one imagining would suppose any kind of association at all, or it was placed in a way that hints at what they turned away from, namely monotheism, toward what they committed, which brought upon them the threat, namely associationism. Or it may be said: He made the pronoun singular in (I will surely fill) because filling has no plurality in it, so the singular pronoun is more fitting to it. The same may be said regarding ﴿the word from Me has come true﴾; and giving multiplies with the multiplicity of the recipients, so the pronoun of majesty is more fitting to it. The same may be said of its counterpart in (We willed). Reflect on this. And it does not follow from His words (all together) that all of the jinn and mankind enter it. As for His words, the Exalted: ﴿And there is none of you but will come to it﴾ [Maryam: 71], the coming there is other than entering, and the discussion of that has already passed, because (all together) indicates the generality of kinds, not of individuals. So the meaning is: "I will surely fill it from these two kinds together," just as one fills a bag with dirhams and dinars together. This has been said, but it was refuted: if this were intended, the fitting form would have been the dual rather than the plural, by saying "both of them" (kiláhuma). It has been deemed preferable that it indicates the generality of individuals. The definiteness in (the jinn and the men) is for the specific reference, and what is meant is their disobedient ones. This is supported by the verse containing the address to Iblis. The sum of the verse: "If We had willed to give every soul its guidance, We would have given it to it; but the word from Me has come true: I will surely fill Hell, etc. Accordingly, by that word, We did not will to give guidance to all in general; rather We prevented it from the followers of Iblis, of whom you are among the number, since you directed your choice to error by his misleading. Our will regarding the acts of servants is bound to their choosing them. So when you did not choose guidance and chose misguidance, We did not will to give it to you. We gave it only to those who chose it from among the righteous, and they are the ones meant by what will come, God willing, in His words, glorified is He: ﴿Only those believe in Our signs﴾ — the verse…"
Page 129
So the real ground for His, the Exalted's, not willing to give guidance is in truth their evil choice, not the realization of the word. The will was restricted by what has passed of the active relation to the acts of servants at the moment of their occurrence, because the eternal will, insofar as it relates to what will occur from their acts in summary, precedes the realization of the word of punishment; so its absence is not contingent upon its realization. Its real ground is His, the Exalted's, knowledge that He will not turn their choice in what is to come toward error, and their preferring it over guidance. So if the will were meant from that aspect, it would be countered by its absence, by saying: "But We did not will," and it would be tied to the ground mentioned, in the manner of His words, the Exalted: ﴿Had God known any good in them, He would have made them hear﴾ [al-Anfal: 23]. Thus said some of the eminent scholars.

It may be said: it is permissible that by the will is meant the eternal will insofar as it relates to what will occur from their acts, and by the word is meant God's knowledge, for it, and likewise the word of God, glorified is He, is applied to that, as al-Raghib said, and he cited from it His words, the Exalted: ﴿The word has certainly come true upon most of them, so they do not believe﴾ [Ya-Sin: 7], and His words, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed, those upon whom the word of your Lord has come true will not believe﴾ [Yunus: 96]. The sum of the meaning: "If We had willed, from eternity, to give every soul its guidance in this world, We would have given it to it; but My knowledge had been established and realized from eternity regarding the punishment of the disobedient. Accordingly, We did not will, since the known must necessarily occur in conformity with the knowledge, lest knowledge turn into ignorance. The occurrence of that requires the existence of the disobedient, since the punishment of the disobedient is a branch of their existence. And the will to give guidance to every soul entails the obedience of every soul, by the necessity of the cause entailing the effect; so the punished soul would have to be both disobedient and obedient, which is impossible. This impossibility arose from His will to give every soul its guidance together with His knowledge of the punishment of the disobedient. Either the said knowledge is negated, which is impossible, because the connection of His, glorified is He, knowledge to the known as it is, is necessary; so the absence of the will for that is determined. This is strengthened by the ultimate conclusion that the cause of the absence of His will to give guidance to the disobedient is the evil of what they are in themselves, because the will follows knowledge, and knowledge follows the known in itself. So His, the Exalted's, knowledge of the punishment of the disobedient requires His, glorified is He, knowledge of them under the heading of their being disobedient, so He does not will them, majestic is His majesty, except under this heading which is established for them in themselves, and He does not will them, glorified is He, contrary to it, because His, the Exalted's, will for them as such would require the connection of knowledge to a thing contrary to what it is in the reality of the matter, and that is not knowledge."

"It is possible that knowledge remains on its apparent sense, and it may be said: He, the Exalted, did not will their guidance because He, exalted is He, said to Iblis, may the curse be upon him, that He, glorified is He, punishes his followers, and it must be so, and the Exalted does not say the opposite of what He knows. So He, blessed and exalted, does not will the opposite of what He says. And it ultimately returns, upon slight reflection, also to His, the Exalted's, not willing their guidance because of the evil of what they are in themselves. The consequence of the answer on both explanations is: there is no benefit for you in returning, because of the evil of what you are in yourselves. It is not hidden that what has been mentioned is built upon the doctrine of fixed essences, and that the wretched is wretched in himself, and the happy is happy in himself, and God's, the Exalted's, knowledge relates to both as they are in themselves, and His, glorified is He, will relates to bringing both into being in accordance with what He, majestic is His majesty, knew; so they came into existence in the external world by His, the Exalted's, bringing them into being as they are in themselves. When this is established, that is established; otherwise, not."

And the fa' in His, the Exalted's, words:

[Fa-dhuqu] ﴿So taste﴾ marks the sequencing of the command to taste, following what is implied by the statement about denying a return to the world, or following His words, ﴿But the Word from Me has come into effect﴾ and so on. Perhaps this is the more immediately apparent reading. Some have taken it to be the response (jawab) to an implied conditional clause (shart muqaddar), meaning: "When you despair of returning, or when the word has come into effect, then taste." It is also permitted for it to be an elaborative clause (tafsiliyya), with the command serving as a threat and rebuke. The particle "bi" in His words, glorified is He, ﴿because you forgot the meeting of this your Day﴾, indicates causation, and "ma" is a verbal-noun particle (masdariyya). This phrase is a qualifier of "Day" (yawm), introduced for the sake of awe-inspiring terror. It is also permitted that it be the object of "dhuqu" (taste), referring to their present state of bowed heads, disgrace, and grief. According to the first reading, the object of "dhuqu" is omitted, and the qualifying reading is more apparent, meaning: "So taste because of your forgetting the meeting of this awesome Day, and your abandoning reflection upon it and provision for it entirely." This is an explicit statement of the cause of the punishment on their part, so it does not preclude that it has another cause, whether real or otherwise. The rebuke for this cause among the other causes is due to its being evident, and because it proceeded from them, so they cannot deny it. The intended meaning of their forgetting that is their abandoning reflection upon it and preparation for it, as we have indicated. In this sense it is voluntary, for which they are rebuked, and it is hardly valid to intend the literal meaning, although rebuke for it is valid in view of deliberately pursuing its cause, namely absorption in following desires. Similar to this, in being a metaphor, is the forgetting in His words: ﴿Indeed, We have forgotten you﴾, meaning: We have left you in punishment with the complete abandonment of one who is forgotten. Some have considered this to be a case of mushakala (rhetorical correspondence). The fact that the first usage is a metaphor was not considered an obstacle to it. It is said that the indication of intended mushakala here is that their recompense was intended to be of the same kind as their deed, so it is in the manner of His words: ﴿And the recompense for an evil deed is an evil deed like it﴾ [al-Shura 42:40]. His words, exalted is He, ﴿And taste the punishment of eternity because of what you used to do﴾, are a repetition for emphasis and intensification. Specifying the ambiguous object of "taste," and signalling that its cause is not merely the forgetting mentioned, but rather other causes of various kinds of disbelief and sins that they persisted in during the world, and since this contains an addition beyond the first, it acquires a distinction from it, which justifies its conjunction with it. The whole was not arranged in a single series, in order to draw attention to the independence of each of the forgetting and what is mentioned as deserving punishment, and to the ambiguity of the tasted object at first and its clarification second, through the repetition of the command and the insertion of the resumptive (isti'naf) clause that indicates complete wrath between them, which conveys, as is not hidden, the utmost severity in taking vengeance upon them.
