Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 32, verse 15:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Only those believe in Our signs who, when they are reminded of them, fall down in prostration﴾. This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) brought to establish that they do not deserve to be granted guidance, and to indicate that they would not believe even if it were granted to them, by specifying those who deserve it through the form of restriction (qasr). It is as if it were said: "You do not believe in Our signs, which indicate Our affairs, nor do you act righteously in accordance with what they require, even if We returned you to the world." And ﴿those who, when they are reminded of them﴾, that is, when they are admonished, ﴿fall down in prostration﴾, (kharru sujjadan) immediately, as a thing falls at once, without hesitation or stammering, let alone procrastination until they witness what the promise and warning they have heard speak of; that is, they fall prostrate, humbling themselves before God, Exalted is He, and out of submissiveness and fear of His punishment, Mighty and Majestic is He. Abu Hayyan said: "This prostration is one of the obligatory prostrations of the Qur'an." Ibn 'Abbas said: "Prostration (sujud) here means bowing (ruku')."

It is narrated from Ibn Jurayj and Mujahid that the verse was revealed concerning a group of hypocrites who, whenever the prayer was called, would leave the mosque, so bowing was intended by this. It would follow from this that the verse is Medinan. From the school of Ibn 'Abbas is that the reciter of a prostration verse should bow, and he cited His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And he fell down bowing and turned in repentance﴾ [Sad: 24]. End quote.

The argument from this is not free of objection. ﴿And they glorify the praise of their Lord﴾, that is, they declare Him far above, at that moment, everything that is unbefitting to Him, Glorified is He, among which is inability to resurrect, while being joined with praise of Him, Exalted is He, for His blessings, Majestic and Exalted is He, for which guidance is granted through the bestowal of signs and the enabling to be guided by them. Thus, the praise (hamd) corresponds to the blessing, the preposition (ba') denotes accompaniment, and the prepositional phrase is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). The mention of the title of Lordship (rububiyyah), by way of iltifat (shift of discourse), together with its addition to their pronoun, indicates the cause of the glorification and praise: that they perform both with awareness of His Lordship over them. ﴿And they are not arrogant﴾ toward faith and obedience, as one does who persists in arrogance, as if he had not heard the signs. The clause is either coordinated with the relative clause, or is a circumstantial clause from one of the two pronouns in (kharru and sabbahu). Its coordination with one of the two verbs has also been permitted.

وقولُه تعالى: ﴿تَتَجافى جُنُوبُهم عَنِ المَضاجِعِ﴾ جملةٌ مستأنفةٌ (*mustanifah*, a new sentence that is not grammatically linked to what precedes it) لبيانِ بقيةِ محاسنِهم.

وجُوِّز أن تكونَ حاليةً (*ḥāliyyah*, a circumstantial clause), أو خبرًا ثانيًا للمبتدأ، والتجافي البُعدُ والارتفاعُ، والجنوبُ جمعُ جَنْبٍ الشُّقوقُ، وذكرَ [Page 131] الراغبُ أنَّ أصلَ الجنبِ الجارحةُ، ثم يُستعارُ في الناحيةِ التي تَليها، كعادتِهم في استعارةِ سائرِ الجوارحِ لذلك، نحو اليمينِ والشمالِ. (والمضاجعُ) جمعُ المضجعِ، أماكنُ الاتكاءِ للنومِ، أي تتنحّى وترتفعُ جنوبُهم عن مواضعِ النومِ، وهذا كنايةٌ عن تركِهمُ النومَ. ومثلُه قولُ عبدِ اللهِ بنِ رواحةَ يصفُ النبيَّ (ﷺ):

نبيٌّ تجافى جنبُهُ عن فراشِهِ ... إذا استثقلتْ بالمشركينَ المضاجعُ

والمشهورُ أنَّ المرادَ بذلك التجافي القيامُ لصلاةِ النوافلِ (*nawāfil*, supererogatory prayers) باللَّيلِ، وهو قولُ الحسنِ، ومجاهدٍ، ومالكٍ، والأوزاعيِّ، وغيرِهم. وفي الأخبارِ الصحيحةِ ما يشهدُ له،

أخرجَ أحمدُ، والترمذيُّ وصحَّحه، والنسائيُّ، وابنُ ماجهْ، ومحمدُ بنُ نصرٍ في كتابِ الصلاةِ، وابنُ جريرٍ، وابنُ أبي حاتمٍ، والحاكمُ وصحَّحه، وابنُ مردويهِ، والبيهقيُّ في شُعَبِ الإيمانِ، عن مُعاذِ بنِ جبلٍ قال: «كنتُ مع النبيِّ (ﷺ) في سفرٍ، فأصبحتُ يومًا قريبًا منه، ونحنُ نسيرُ، فقلتُ: يا نبيَّ اللهِ، أخبرْني بعملٍ يُدخلُني الجنةَ ويُباعدُني من النارِ؟ قال: لقد سألتَ عن عظيمٍ، وإنه ليسيرٌ على مَن يسَّره اللهُ عليه، تعبدُ اللهَ ولا تُشركُ به شيئًا، وتُقيمُ الصلاةَ، وتُؤتي الزكاةَ، وتصومُ رمضانَ، وتحجُّ البيتَ. ثم قال: ألا أدلُّكَ على أبوابِ الخيرِ؟ الصومُ جُنّةٌ، والصدقةُ تُطفئُ الخطيئةَ، وصلاةُ الرجلِ في جوفِ الليلِ. ثم قرأ: ﴿تَتَجافى جُنُوبُهم عَنِ المَضاجِعِ﴾ حتى بلغَ ﴿يَعْمَلُونَ﴾» الحديثَ.

وقال أبو الدرداءِ، وقتادةُ، والضحاكُ: هو أن يصلِّيَ الرجلُ العشاءَ والصبحَ في جماعةٍ. وعن الحسنِ، وعطاءٍ: هو أن لا ينامَ الرجلُ حتى يصلِّيَ العشاءَ. أخرجَ الترمذيُّ وصحَّحه، وابنُ جريرٍ، وغيرُهما، عن أنسٍ قال: إنَّ هذه الآيةَ ﴿تَتَجافى جُنُوبُهم عَنِ المَضاجِعِ﴾ نزلتْ في انتظارِ الصلاةِ التي تُدعى العَتَمةَ (*ʿatamah*, the night prayer, i.e. ʿIshāʾ). وفي روايةٍ أخرى عنه أنه قال فيها: «نزلتْ فينا معاشرَ الأنصارِ، كنّا نصلي المغربَ، فلا نرجعُ إلى رحالِنا حتى نصليَ العشاءَ مع النبيِّ (ﷺ)». وقيل: هو أن يصلِّيَ الرجلُ المغربَ، ويصلِّيَ بعدها إلى العشاءِ، فقد أخرجَ عبدُ اللهِ بنُ أحمدَ في زوائدِ الزهدِ (*Zawāʾid al-Zuhd*), وابنُ عديٍّ، وابنُ مردويهِ، عن مالكِ بنِ دينارٍ قال: «سألتُ أنسَ بنَ مالكٍ عن هذه الآيةِ: ﴿تَتَجافى جُنُوبُهم عَنِ المَضاجِعِ﴾ قال: كان قومٌ من أصحابِ رسولِ اللهِ (ﷺ) من المهاجرين الأوّلين يصلُّون المغربَ، ويصلُّون بعدها إلى عِشاءِ الآخرةِ، فنزلتْ هذه الآيةُ فيهم». وقال قتادةُ، وعكرمةُ: هو أن يصلِّيَ الرجلُ ما بين المغربِ والعشاءِ، واستدلَّ له بما أخرجَهُ محمدُ بنُ نصرٍ، عن عبدِ اللهِ بنِ عيسى قال: كان ناسٌ من الأنصارِ يصلُّون ما بين المغربِ والعشاءِ، فنزلتْ فيهم: ﴿تَتَجافى جُنُوبُهم عَنِ المَضاجِعِ﴾.

وأخرجَ ابنُ جريرٍ، عن ابنِ عباسٍ رضي الله عنهما أنه قال في الآيةِ: ﴿تَتَجافى جُنُوبُهم﴾ لذكرِ اللهِ تعالى، كلما استيقظوا ذكروا اللهَ عزَّ وجلَّ، إما في الصلاةِ، وإما في قيامٍ، أو قعودٍ، أو على جُنوبِهم، لا يزالون يذكرون اللهَ تعالى. ورَوى نحوَه هو ومحمدُ بنُ نصرٍ، عن الضحاكِ. والجمهورُ عوَّلوا على ما هو المشهورُ، وفي فضلِ التهجُّدِ (*tahajjud*, night prayer) ما لا يُحصى من الأخبارِ، وأفضلُه على ما نصَّ عليه غيرُ واحدٍ ما كان في الأسحارِ.

﴿يَدْعُونَ رَبَّهم﴾ حالٌ من ضميرِ ﴿جُنُوبُهم﴾، وقد أُضيفَ إليه ما هو جزءٌ، وجُوِّز على احتمالِ كونِ جملةِ ﴿تَتَجافى﴾ إلخ حاليةً أن تكونَ حالًا ثانيةً مما جُعلتْ تلك حالًا منه، وعلى احتمالِ كونِها خبرًا ثانيًا للمبتدأ، أن تكونَ خبرًا ثالثًا، وجُوِّز كونُها مستأنفةً. والظاهرُ أنَّ المرادَ بدعائِهم ربَّهم سبحانَه المعنى المتبادرُ، وقيل: المرادُ به الصلاةُ. ﴿خَوْفًا﴾ أي خائفينَ من سُخطِه تعالى، وعذابِه عزَّ وجلَّ وعدمِ قبولِ عبادتِهم، ﴿وَطَمَعًا﴾ [Page 132] في رحمتِه تباركَ وتعالى. فالمصدرانِ حالانِ من ضميرِ ﴿يَدْعُونَ﴾، وجُوِّز أن يكونا مصدرَيْنِ لمقدَّرٍ، أي يخافون خوفًا ويطمعون طمعًا، وتكونُ الجملةُ حينئذٍ حالًا، وأن يكونا مفعولًا له. ولا يخفى أنَّ الآيةَ على الحاليةِ أمدحُ.

﴿وَمِمَّا رَزَقْناهُمْ﴾ إيّاهُ من المالِ ﴿يُنْفِقُونَ﴾ في وجوهِ الخيرِ.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 32, verse 17:

﴿So no soul knows﴾ meaning: every soul among souls, neither a near-brought angel nor a sent prophet, let alone others than them, for an indefinite noun in the context of negation is general. The fa' is either causal (sababiyyah) or expository (fasihah), meaning: they were given beyond their hope. ﴿So no soul knows﴾ ﴿what has been concealed for them﴾, meaning for those whose noble attributes were enumerated, ﴿of comfort for the eyes﴾, meaning that which eyes are comforted by. Attributing "comfort" (qurrah) to "the eyes" in general, rather than to "their eyes," is an indication that what has been concealed for them is of the utmost excellence and perfection.

Al-Shaykhan and others narrated from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: Allah the Exalted says: "I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived, apart from what I have revealed to you. Recite, if you wish: (So no soul knows what has been concealed for them of comfort for the eyes)."

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and al-Hakim, who declared it sound, narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "It is indeed written in the Torah: 'Allah the Exalted has prepared for those whose sides forsake their beds what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and it has not occurred to the heart of any human.'" And no near-brought angel or sent prophet knows it, and it is indeed in the Qur'an: ﴿So no soul knows what has been concealed for them of comfort for the eyes﴾,
﴿as a reward for what they used to do﴾, meaning: they are recompensed for what they used to do of righteous deeds. (Jaza'an) is an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) of a implied verb, and the sentence is resumed (mustanif'ah).

It is permitted to make it a circumstantial (ḥāliyyah) clause. It was also said: it is permissible to make it an emphatic verbal noun (maṣdar mu'akkid) for the content of the preceding sentence. It was also said: it may be an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu) for the saying of the Exalted, ﴿So no soul knows﴾, meaning: they were prevented from knowing it because of the recompense, or because of "concealed," for its concealment is due to the greatness of its rank. From al-Hasan, he said: The people concealed deeds in this world, so Allah the Exalted concealed for them what no eye has seen and no ear has heard, meaning He concealed that so that the recompense would be of the same kind as the deed.

In al-Kashshaf it is stated that this indicates the fa' in the saying of the Exalted, ﴿So no soul knows﴾, is a connective linking the more fitting (al-ahaqq) with what precedes, and its original form is "so they do not know," and the shift is for magnifying the recompense, and the omission of the agent in (ukhfiya) is a reinforcement of it, because its recompenser is the Great One alone, so it does not go elsewhere, and is there any going to other than Him, glorified be He? End of quote. So reflect.

Hamzah, Ya'qub, and al-A'mash read "akhfi" with a sukun on the yā' as a present-tense verb of the first-person speaker. Ibn Mas'ud read "nukhfi" with the royal "we." Al-A'mash also read "akhfaytu" attributed to the first-person singular speaker alone. Muhammad ibn Ka'b read (akhfa) as a past-tense verb in the active voice.

(Ma) in all of these is a relative pronoun (ism mawsul), the object of (ta'lamu), and knowledge here means cognition (ma'rifah). The returning pronoun is the implicit pronoun serving as the deputy of the agent according to the reading of the majority, and its pronoun is omitted according to other readings. Abu al-Baqa' said: (ma) may be an interrogative, in which case its position is nominative as subject, and (ukhfiya lahum) is its predicate according to the reading of one who vocalizes the yā' with a fatḥah; and according to the reading of one who vocalizes it with a sukun, making (ukhfi) a present-tense verb, (ma) is in the accusative position governed by (akhfa). (Ya'lamu) from it indicates its state according to the rest of the readings. When it is interrogative, knowledge may be in the sense of cognition, or it may be in its literal sense, in which case it takes two objects, which the interrogative clause fills; and under either possibility, whether relative or interrogative, the vagueness serves to magnify.

ʿAbd Allah, Abu al-Darda', Abu Hurayrah, ʿAwn, and al-ʿUqayli read "min qurrāt" in the plural with the alif and tā', and this is a narration from Abu ʿAmr, Abu Ja'far, and al-A'mash. The plural of the verbal noun or its noun form is due to the differing kinds of comfort, and the prepositional phrase is in the position of a circumstantial clause.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 32, verse 18:

﴿Is one who was a believer like one who was defiant?﴾ That is: after the clear distinction between the two has become evident, is it supposed that the believer, whose virtuous attributes have been related, is like the defiant one, whose corrupt and worthless conditions have been mentioned? The origin of fisq (defiance, transgression) is "khurūj" (going out), from "fasaqat al-thamarah" when the fruit came out of its skin. Then it was used for going out of obedience and of the rulings of the Sharia in general, so it is broader than kufr (disbelief), though it may be restricted to it, as in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And whoever disbelieves after that, those are the defiant ones﴾ [al-Nur: 55], and as here, because it is set against "believer", along with what you will hear after this, God willing. ﴿They are not equal﴾: the explicit statement of this, together with the implication of denial, is to negate resemblance entirely, in the most eloquent and emphatic manner, for added emphasis, and so that the detail that follows may be built upon it. The plural is used in view of the meaning of "man" (man), just as the singular in what preceded was in view of its wording. It has also been said: the pronoun refers to two, namely the believer and the disbeliever, and the dual is a plural.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 32, verse 19:

﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, for them are the Gardens of Refuge﴾ is an elaboration of the ranks of the two groups after the negation of their equality. It has also been said: it comes after the mention of their conditions in this world. The gardens are attributed to "the refuge" because they are the true refuge and the real dwelling, while this world is a station from which one will inevitably depart. It has also been said that "al-Ma'wa" is a proper name for a specific place among the gardens, like ʿAdn. It has also been said that "Jannat al-Ma'wa" (the Garden of Refuge) is so named on the basis of what is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, that the spirits of the martyrs take refuge in it, and it is related that it lies to the right of the Throne. The distance of making it a proper name is not hidden. In any case, it is not far-fetched that there is in this an allusion to what was mentioned of their withdrawing from their beds, which are their refuge in this world.

Ṭalḥa read «Jannatu al-Ma'wā» in the singular. ﴿Nuzulan﴾ means reward. Originally it refers to the food, drink and provisions prepared for a guest who arrives, and then it became general for every gift. It is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of "Jannāt", and the governing element in it is the adverbial phrase. It has also been permitted that it be the plural of nāzil (guest), in which case it is a circumstantial qualifier of the pronoun in "alladhīna āmanū". Abu Ḥaywa read «Nuzlan» with a sukūn on the zāy, as in the verse:

"And when the tyrant came upon us with his army, we made the spears and the sharp swords his nuzl (provision)."

﴿Bima kānū yaʿmalūn﴾ means: because of what they used to do in the world of righteous deeds, taking "mā" as a relative pronoun, with the returning pronoun omitted, and the "bā'" being causal. That this is a cause is by the requirement of His exalted grace and His promise, mighty and majestic, and so it does not contradict the hadith, "None of you enters Paradise by his deeds." The "bā'" may also be for exchange and opposition, like "ʿalā" in the phrase: "I sold you the house for a thousand dirhams," meaning: for them is that in return for what they used to do.

﴿As for those who defied (transgressed)﴾, i.e., they went out of obedience, so they disbelieved and committed sins, ﴿then their refuge is﴾, i.e., their dwelling and place, ﴿the Fire﴾. Some scholars have mentioned that "al-ma'wa" (refuge) has become customarily used for that in which a person seeks shelter and a resting place where he finds relief from heat and cold, even if only imaginarily. So when it is intended here, there is a sarcastic metaphor (isti'arah tahakkumiyyah) in the speech, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so give them tidings of a painful punishment﴾ [Al 'Imran: 21; At-Tawbah: 34; Al-Inshiqaq: 24]. It has also been permitted that the use of this word is by way of correspondence (mushakalah), because when He mentioned in one of the two categories ﴿for them are the gardens of refuge﴾, He mentioned in the other ﴿their refuge is the Fire﴾. ﴿Whenever they wish to get out of it, they are returned to it﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining how the Fire is their refuge. The speech is in the manner of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿a wall that wishes to collapse﴾ [Al-Kahf: 77], according to what has been said. The meaning is: whenever they approach leaving it and come close to it, they are returned into it and pushed down to its bottom.

It has been narrated that the flame of the Fire strikes them so that they rise to its top, until, when they come near its gate and wish to exit from it, the flame strikes them and they fall down to its bottom, and so they are treated forever.

It has also been said: the speech is on its apparent meaning, but there is an ellipsis in it, i.e.,
[p. 134]
whenever they wish to exit from it, and they exit from most of it, they are returned into it. What points to their exit from most of it is His saying, ﴿in it﴾ rather than ﴿into it﴾. It has also been permitted that the speech here is an expression of their eternal abiding in it. In any case, there is no contradiction between this verse and His saying: ﴿and they will never be out of the Fire﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 167]. ﴿And it will be said to them﴾ as an intensification against them and an increase in their rage.

﴿Taste the punishment of the Fire which you used to deny﴾, i.e., the punishment of the Fire ﴿you used to deny﴾ continually in the world. The Fire is mentioned explicitly, although it was mentioned before, for the sake of increasing the threat and intimidation and magnifying the matter. Ibn al-Hajib, in his Amali, mentioned another reason for the explicit mention, which is that the sentence that follows the saying is a report of what will be said to them on the Day of Resurrection when they wish to exit the Fire. Therefore, placing a pronoun does not suit that, since the saying at that time is not preceded by a mention of the Fire. Rather, He, glorified is He, mentioned it earlier as information about their states. Al-Tibi, may God have mercy on him, examined this, saying: this saying is also included in the domain of information, because it is conjoined to ﴿they are returned﴾, which is the response to "whenever" (kullama). So just as a pronoun was permissible in the conjoined-to clause, it is also permissible in this one, if the increase of threat and intimidation is not intended.

It was answered that what prevents it is that it is a report of what will be said to them on the Day of Resurrection, and the basic principle in reporting is that it should conform to the one reported from, without alteration or pronominalization in the reported speech, since the Fire was not previously mentioned in it. And it was objected to that this may be contested, since his meaning is that it is permissible to observe the reported speech and the reporting, and just as the basic principle is observing the reported speech, the basic principle is pronominalization if the mention has preceded, so a preponderant factor is needed.

Some verifying scholars said: Ibn al-Hajib meant that explicit mention is the more suitable in this sentence, considering its own nature and considering its context. As for the first: it is because it is said without the Fire having been previously mentioned. As for the second: the context of the verse is for threat, intimidation, and magnifying the matter, and explicit mention contains of that what pronominalization does not. This is far from being refuted by al-Tibi's objection. The fair view is that both pronominalization and explicit mention are permissible, and that he preferred explicit mention because the context requires it. It is reported from al-Raghib what indicates that the situation in this verse is a situation calling for a pronoun, since it was mentioned from him that he said in Durrat al-Tanzil: He, exalted is He, said here ﴿Taste the punishment of the Fire which you used to deny﴾, and He, glorified is He, said in another verse: ﴿the punishment of the Fire which you used to deny﴾ [Saba': 42]. So here He used the masculine, and there He used the feminine. The secret of this is that the Fire here came in the position of a pronoun, and a pronoun is not described, so the description was applied to the punishment attributed to it, which is masculine. In that verse, the Fire was not mentioned in its context, so the Fire did not come in the position of a pronoun, and the description was applied to it, and it is feminine, not the punishment. So reflect.

﴿And We will surely make them taste of the nearer punishment﴾, i.e., the closer one. It was also said: the lesser one, and this is the punishment of this world, for it is closer than the punishment of the Hereafter and lesser than it. Scholars differed about what is meant by it. Al-Nasa'i and a group related, and al-Hakim authenticated, from Ibn Mas'ud that it is the years of famine that afflicted them. This is also reported from al-Nakha'i and Muqatil. Al-Tabarani and others related, and al-Hakim authenticated, also from Ibn Mas'ud, that it is what befell them on the Day of Badr. Something similar is reported from al-Hasan ibn Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, with the wording being the killing by the sword, like the Day of Badr. From Mujahid, it is killing and hunger.

Muslim, Abdullah ibn Ahmad in the Zawa'id of the Musnad, Abu 'Awana in his Sahih, and others related from Ubayy ibn Ka'b that he said: "It is the calamities of this world, the Romans, the assault (al-batshah), and the smoke." In Muslim's wording: "or the smoke."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Jarir related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "It is the calamities of this world, its illnesses, and its afflictions." In another narration from him and from al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd, with the wording: "the calamities of this world in one's self and one's wealth." In the same meaning is what Ibn Mardawayh related: "From Abu Idris al-Khawlani, who said: I asked 'Ubada ibn al-Samit about the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And We will surely make them taste﴾ (the verse), and he said: I asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about it, and he ﷺ said: 'It is the calamities, the illnesses, and the burdens (al-asar), a punishment for the one who transgresses in this world, short of the punishment of the Hereafter.' I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, then what is it for us?' He said: 'Expiation and purification.'" [Page 135] In another narration from Ibn 'Abbas, it is the prescribed punishments (al-hudud).

Here Abu 'Ubayda related from him that he explained it as the punishment of the grave. It is also transmitted from Mujahid: ﴿short of the greater punishment﴾ is the punishment of the Day of Resurrection, as was reported from Ibn Mas'ud and others. Ibn 'Atiyya said: there is no disagreement that this is what is meant. In al-Tahrir it is said: most of them hold that the greater punishment is the punishment of the Day of Resurrection in the Fire. It was also said: it is the killing, the taking captive, and the imprisonment.

And from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, may Allah be pleased with them both, that it is the emergence of the Mahdi with the sword. End of quotation.

Based on these two, the nearer punishment is explained as years of famine, or illnesses, or the like, which is nearer than what has been mentioned. From some of the People of the House it is explained as the Beast (al-Dabba) and the Dajjal. The reliance is upon what most scholars hold.

Why did the verse not say "the lesser" in contrast to "the greater", or "the farther" in contrast to "the nearer"? Because the purpose is intimidation and warning, and that is achieved through proximity, not through smallness, and through greatness, not through distance. This was stated by al-Naysaburi, summarizing it from the words of al-Imam. Abu Hayyan likewise affirmed this, except that he said: the nearer includes the lesser, because it ends with the death of the one punished, and the greater includes the farther, because it occurs in the Hereafter; thus the contrast is achieved through inclusion, and he expressed what is more emphatic in intimidation.

﴿That perhaps they may return﴾, i.e., that perhaps those who remain among them may repent. This was stated by Ibn Mas'ud. Al-Zamakhshari said: or that perhaps they may desire to return and seek it, like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Return us, we will do righteousness﴾ [al-Sajda: 12]. The desire to return has been called a return, just as the desire to stand has been called standing in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿When you rise to prayer, wash your faces﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 6]. This is supported by the reading of the one who read "yurja'un" in the passive voice. End of quotation.

This is according to what is related from Mujahid and reported from Abu 'Ubayda. So "perhaps" (la'alla-hum) and what follows is connected to His saying, the Exalted, ﴿And We will surely make them taste of the nearer punishment﴾, as in the first interpretation, except that the return there is repentance, while here the return is to the world. It would be of the type of ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [al-Qasas: 8]. Or the hope (al-tarajji) may refer back to them. The indication of the mentioned reading upon this is that it is not valid to carry it upon repentance in it. The apparent meaning is the transmitted explanation, and the reading does not contradict it, since it is permissible that the meaning be: "that this punishment may bring them back from disbelief to faith." And "la'alla" expresses the hope of the addressees, as Sibawayh explained it. From Ibn 'Abbas, its explanation here is "kay" (in order that), and it seems the intended meaning is: "in order that We may expose them through that to repentance." Al-Zamakhshari made it an expression of His hope, the Exalted, and since the reality of that is impossible for Him, the Mighty and Majestic, he took it to mean His will, the Exalted. He raised an objection to this and answered it according to his Mu'tazili doctrine, so do not pay attention to it.

Now, the verses from His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Is one who was a believer like one who was defiant?﴾ up to here were revealed concerning 'Ali, may Allah honor his face, and al-Walid ibn 'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt, the half-brother of 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, may Allah be pleased with him, through his mother Urwa bint Kurayz ibn Rabi'a ibn Habib ibn 'Abd Shams.

Abu al-Faraj al-Isbahani in the Kitab al-Aghani, al-Wahidi, Ibn 'Adi, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Khatib, and Ibn 'Asakir related through various chains from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: al-Walid ibn 'Uqba said to 'Ali, may Allah honor his face: "I am sharper than you in spear-point, more expansive than you in tongue, and fuller than you in the ranks of the army." 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Be silent, for you are only a defiant one (fasiq)." So the verse ﴿Is one who was a believer...﴾ etc. was revealed.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi something similar. He also related this from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla, that it was revealed concerning 'Ali, may Allah honor his face, and al-Walid ibn 'Uqba, but he did not mention what occurred.

In another narration from him, it was revealed concerning 'Ali, may Allah honor his face, and a man from Quraysh, whom he did not name.

In al-Kashshaf it is narrated concerning its revelation that "a dispute occurred between 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, and al-Walid ibn 'Uqba on the Day of Badr. Al-Walid said to him: 'Be silent, for you are a child; I am more youthful than you in youth, stronger than you in strength, sharper than you in tongue, sharper than you in spear-point, braver than you in heart, and fuller than you in filling the ranks of the army.' 'Ali, may Allah honor his face, said to him: 'Be silent, for you are a defiant one (fasiq),' so it was revealed."

We have not seen it with this wording in a chain of narration (musnad). Al-Khafaji said: Ibn Hajar said: it is a gross error, for al-Walid was not a man on the Day of Badr, but a child, and it is inconceivable that he attended Badr and did what was mentioned.

Al-Jalal al-Suyuti quoted from Shaykh Wali al-Din: it is not sound, for al-Walid was too young for that. I say: some reports indicate that he was not born on the Day of Badr, or that he was very young. Abu Dawud related in the Sunan, through the route of Thabit ibn al-Hajjaj, from Abu Musa 'Abd Allah al-Hamdani, from him (al-Walid), that he said: "When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ conquered Mecca, the people of Mecca began bringing their children to him, and he would wipe over their heads. I was brought to him, peace and blessings be upon him, and I was smeared with perfume (mukhalloq), so he did not touch me because of the perfume." However, Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: Abu Musa is unknown (majhul). Also, al-Zubayr and others among the people of knowledge of the biographies (siyar) mentioned that Umm Kulthum bint 'Uqba, when she emigrated to the Prophet ﷺ during the truce in the year seven, her two brothers al-Walid and 'Umara went out to bring her back. This is apparent in showing that he was not a child on the day of the conquest, for one who is such, how could he be among those who went out to return his sister before the conquest? Some reports indicate that he was a man on the Day of Badr, for al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar mentioned in his book al-Isaba that he came to ransom his paternal cousin al-Harith ibn Abi Wajra ibn Abi 'Amr ibn Umayya, who had been captured on the Day of Badr, and he ransomed him for four thousand. He said: "The people of the campaigns (maghazi) related this," and he did not follow it with anything, and the sense of his speech is apparent in approving it. The implication of that is that what he undertook were the deeds of men, not of children. What we have mentioned from Ibn Hajar contradicts what al-Khafaji, may Allah have mercy on him, reported from him as just passed. It should not be said that he could have been a child on that day, of an age in which attending was customary, so he attended and what occurred did occur, because describing him as a defiant one in the sense of disbelief, and the threat concerning it as you have heard in the verses, while he was under the age of puberty, is something only one who holds that the obligation of faith at that time was conditioned upon discernment would be inclined to. Nor should it be said: it is possible that this story was after his conversion to Islam, and he was called "defiant" while he was a Muslim, as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿O you who believe, if a defiant one brings you news, verify it﴾ [al-Hujurat: 6]. For Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: there is no disagreement among the people of knowledge of the interpretation of the Qur'an that it was revealed concerning him, since the Prophet ﷺ sent him as a collector of charity (musaddiq) to the Banu al-Mustaliq, and he returned and reported that they had apostatized and withheld the charity, and the matter was not as he said, because the defiance here means disbelief, while there it is not so. Then know that the claim that it was revealed concerning 'Ali, may Allah honor his face, and al-Walid, because of a dispute that occurred on the Day of Badr, implies that it is Medinan, while the preferred opinion of some of them is otherwise.

[Page 137]

*And who is more unjust than one who is reminded of the signs of his Lord and then turns away from them?* ﴿ومَن أظْلَمُ مِمَّنْ ذُكِّرَ بِآياتِ رَبِّهِ ثُمَّ أعْرَضَ عَنْها﴾ This is a general statement about one who opposes the signs of God Most High with aversion, following the description of one who responds to them with prostration, glorification, and praise. The word *thumma* (then, here indicating a remote or surprising sequence) is used to express that turning away from them is far-fetched by reason, given their utmost clarity and their guidance to the happiness of both worlds, as in the verse of Ja'far ibn 'Ulayyah al-Harithi:

*None relieves the distress except the son of a free woman, who sees the throes of death and then visits them.*

The meaning is that this is more unjust than every wrongdoer. ﴿Indeed, We will take vengeance upon the criminals.﴾ ﴿إنّا مِنَ المُجْرِمِينَ مُنْتَقِمُونَ﴾ It has been said: that is, upon everyone who is characterized by criminality and by acquiring blameworthy matters, even if he is not of this standing. So how about one who is more unjust than every wrongdoer and more gravely criminal than every criminal? Thus, in general, there is an affirmation of vengeance against him by a demonstrative method.

It is permissible that by "the criminal" is meant the aforementioned one who turns away, and the apparent noun has been placed in the position of a pronoun referring back to *man* (who), in view of its meaning. The original would have been: "Indeed, We will take vengeance upon them," to indicate that the cause of vengeance is this aversion's committing such a great crime. Al-Baghawi explained "the criminals" here as "the polytheists." Al-Tibi, may mercy be upon him, said after relating it: "There is no doubt that the discourse is about blaming those who turn away, and this style is more blaming, because it acknowledges that when the disbeliever is described as unjust and criminal, it is taken to the extreme of his disbelief and the utmost of his rebellion, since this verse is like a conclusion to the states of the deniers who say: ﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"?﴾ [al-Sajdah 32:3 and others], and the transition to the story of the Interlocutor (Musa) is a consolation to the heart of the Beloved, upon them both be prayers and peace, to the end of what he mentioned, so let it be consulted."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 32, verse 23:

﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Book﴾, i.e., the genus of the Book. ﴿So do not be in doubt﴾, i.e., in suspicion, ﴿about meeting it﴾, i.e., meeting that genus. Al-Hasan read "miryatin" with a dammah on the mim. ﴿About meeting it﴾, i.e., your meeting with that genus, on the basis that liqa' is a verbal noun (masdar) added to its object, and its subject is omitted, namely the pronoun of the Prophet (ﷺ). The mentioned pronoun refers to the Book, meaning the genus. The giving of that genus is by way of the giving of the Torah, and its meeting is by way of the meeting of the Qur'an. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, you receive the Qur'an from the presence of One Wise and All-Knowing﴾ [al-Naml: 6], and His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And We will bring forth for him on the Day of Resurrection a book he will find spread open﴾ [al-Isra': 13].

Some of them took "al-Kitab" (the Book) to be definite by prior mention, i.e., the known Book, which is the Torah. Since it is not valid for the pronoun to return to it literally, because he (peace and blessings be upon him) did not meet that very Book, it has been said:

The statement is on the basis of an omitted modifier, i.e., the meeting of its like, or on the basis of al-istikhdam (a figure in which one word is used in two senses), or that the pronoun refers to the Qur'an, which is understood from it. There is no concealing the remoteness in each of these. The meaning is: We gave Moses the like of what We gave you of the Book, and We made him meet revelation like what We made you meet of revelation, so do not be in doubt that you met its like and its counterpart. The summary of what the resultative fa' indicates is that your knowledge that Moses (peace be upon him) was given the Torah should be a cause for removing doubt from you regarding the matter of your Book. His prohibition (peace and blessings be upon him) from being in doubt is intended as a prohibition for his community (ﷺ), and an allusion to those who are characterized by it.

It has also been said: the masdar is added to the subject, and the object is omitted, which is his pronoun (peace and blessings be upon him), i.e., of his meeting you and his arrival to you. In the expression "meeting" rather than "giving" there is a magnification of his status (ﷺ) that is not hidden from the one who reflects. It may be said that expressing it in the earlier manner also indicates magnification, but from another aspect, so reflect.

It has also been said: the Book is the Torah, and the pronoun in "liqa'ihi" returns to it without an omitted modifier and without committing istikhdam. ("Liqa'" is a masdar added to its object, and its subject is Moses, i.e., from Moses' meeting the Book, or added to its subject, with its object being Moses, i.e., from the Book's meeting Moses and its arrival to him.) The fa' here is like it in his saying:

"Beauty is not in a wrap-cloth, so know, even if you wear a cloak."

It has entered upon the parenthetical sentence in place of the waw, out of concern for its matter. From al-Hasan: the pronoun in "liqa'ihi" returns to what the discourse contains of hardship and trial that Moses (peace be upon him) encountered. It is as if it were said: And We gave Moses this burden that you are upon the path of, so do not doubt that you will meet with people what he met of hardship and trial. The sentence is parenthetical. Its remoteness is not hidden, and even more remote than this is what has been said:

The pronoun refers to the Angel of Death, who was mentioned earlier, and the sentence is also parenthetical; rather, the speech of Allah, exalted is He, should be exalted above such an interpretation. Al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtarah related with a sound chain from Ibn 'Abbas that he said regarding the verse: i.e., from the meeting of Moses. Ibn al-Mundhir and others related something similar from Mujahid, and Ibn Abi Hatim
page 138
related from Abu al-'Aliyah that he said the same. It was asked of him: Did Moses meet him (peace be upon him)? He said: Yes. Do you not see His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And ask those whom We sent before you of Our messengers﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 45]? And by that he meant his (ﷺ) meeting Moses on the night of the Isra', as mentioned in the two Sahihs and others. Something similar is narrated from Qatadah and a group of the early scholars, and al-Mubarrad said it when he tested al-Zajjaj with this verse. On this view, the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So do not be in doubt about meeting it﴾ is His promise to His Prophet (peace be upon him) of meeting Moses, and the verse would have been revealed before the Isra', and the sentence is parenthetical with fa' in place of waw, as you heard just now.

Making it a consequence of what precedes it is not apparent, and by this some objected to this interpretation. Taking refuge in the interpretation of i'rad (the other sense) is safe from objection, and I think you prefer it over the first interpretation in some respects, and Allah is the Granter of success. ﴿And We made it﴾, i.e., the Book which We gave Moses. Qatadah said: i.e., and We made Moses (peace be upon him) ﴿a guidance﴾, i.e., a guide from misguidance, ﴿for the Children of Israel﴾. They were singled out for mention because they were the most numerous beneficiaries of it. It has also been said: because he (peace be upon him) was not worshipped by what is in his Book, unlike the descendants of Isma'il (ﷺ).

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 32, verse 24:

﴿And We made from among them imams﴾. Qatadah said: "Leaders in goodness, other than the prophets, upon them be peace." It was also said: they are the prophets who were among the Children of Israel. ﴿Guiding﴾ their remnant by what is in the folds of the Book of wisdoms and rulings to the path of truth. Or they guide them to what is in it of the religion of God, exalted and majestic, and His laws, by Our command to them that they should guide, with the *amr* (command) being the singular of *al-awamir* (the commands). This is evident on the view that they were prophets. As for the view that they were not prophets, it is permissible that His command to them to do this be in the manner of the command to the scholars of this community, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And let there be from among you a community who call to good and enjoin what is right﴾, the verse.

It is also permitted that *al-amr* be the singular of *al-umur* (affairs), and that the meaning be "they guide by Our granting success." ﴿When they were patient﴾. Qatadah said: "patient in abandoning the world." Others permitted that the meaning be: when they were patient over the hardships of obedience and enduring difficulties in supporting the religion. (*Lamma*) may be the one that carries the sense of a conditional, as in: "When you honoured me, I honoured you," meaning: when they were patient, We made them imams. It may also be the one that means "when" (*hin*) without the sense of a condition, and the apparent view is that in that case it is an adverbial complement of *ja'alna* (We made), meaning: imams when they were patient. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be an adverbial complement of *yahduna* (they guide).

ʿAbd Allah, Talha, al-A'mash, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Ruways read *limā* with a kasra on the *lam* and a light *mim*, with the *lam* being causal (*lil-ta'lil*) and *ma* being masdariyyah (verbal-noun forming), meaning: because of their patience. This is connected either to *ja'alna* or to *yahduna*. ʿAbd Allah also read *bimā* with the causal *ba'* and the masdariyyah *ma*, meaning: by means of their patience. ﴿And they were certain of Our signs﴾, those which are in the folds of the Book. It was also said that by them is meant what encompasses the cosmic signs. The prepositional phrase is connected to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿they were certain﴾, meaning: they were certain of them because of their deep contemplation of them, not of other false matters. This is an allusion to the disbelievers of Mecca. The clause is conjoined to (*sabaru*, they were patient), so it falls within the scope of (*lamma*). It is permitted that it be conjoined to (*ja'alna*, We made), and that it be in the position of a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in (*sabaru*).

The meaning is similarly: We shall surely make the Book that We gave you, or We shall surely make you a guidance for your community, and We shall surely make from among them imams who guide with the like of that guidance.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 32, verse 25:

﴿Indeed, your Lord — He is the one who will decide﴾ i.e., will judge (yaqḍī) ﴿between them﴾. It has been said: between the prophets, peace be upon them, and their nations.

And it has been said: between the believers and the polytheists ﴿on the Day of Resurrection﴾, so He, glorified is He, will distinguish between the one who is in the right and the one who is in the wrong, ﴿concerning that about which they used to differ﴾ regarding matters of religion.

﴿Has it not been made clear to them?﴾ The hamza is the interrogative particle of rebuke (hamza al-inkar), and the waw is the conjunction of coordination, attached to an implied clause that the context requires, and which the coordinated clause matches in meaning according to the view preferred by more than one scholar. The verb of guidance (fi'l al-hidayah) is either of the type of "so-and-so gives," in that the intended meaning is the act itself without considering an object, or it means "to make clear" (al-tabyin), with the object omitted and the subject a pronoun referring to what is in the mind. This is explained by the words of God, exalted is He: ﴿How many generations did We destroy before them?﴾. The phrase "kam" (how many) is in the accusative position, governed by "ahlakna" (We destroyed). The meaning is: they were heedless and did not let the guidance reach them, or it did not make clear to them the outcome of their affair or the path of truth, namely the multitude of those We destroyed, or the multitude of destruction of those We destroyed from the past generations, such as 'Ad, Thamud, and the people of Lot.

It is not permitted for "kam" to be the subject, because it begins the sentence, as al-Zajjaj stated, transmitting this from the Basrans. Al-Farra' said: "kam" is in the nominative position, governed by "yahdi" (it makes clear), as if you said: "Has it not been made clear to them, the destroyed generations, so that they might take warning?" It is also not permitted for the subject to be elided, because the subject is elided only in specific positions, and this is not one of them. Nor is it a pronoun referring to what comes after, because that would require a pronoun to refer to something later in both wording and rank, in a place where this is not permitted. Nor is the clause itself the subject, since according to the sound view a clause is not the subject unless its wording is intended, as in: "Lā ilāha illā Allāh" (There is no god but God) preserves blood and property. It is permitted for the subject to be a pronoun referring to God, exalted is His majesty, because His mention preceded in the words of God: (Indeed your Lord) etc. This is supported by the reading of Zayd: "Nahdi lahum" (We make clear to them), with the plural of majesty. Al-Khafaji said: the verb with "kam" is in place of the object, which is the content of the clause, because it includes the meaning of knowledge, so do not overlook this.

﴿Walking in their dwellings﴾: that is, they pass by their marketplaces and over their abodes and lands and observe the traces of their destruction. The clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "lahum," and it was said: from "al-qurun" (the generations). The meaning is: We destroyed them while they were in their heedlessness. It was also said: it is a resumptive clause explaining the manner of their guidance.

Ibn al-Sumayqa read "yumashshūna" with the doubled letter, as a form of the verb "mashā" (to walk) indicating intensity. ﴿Indeed in that﴾: that is, in what has been mentioned of Our destruction of the former, defiant nations, or in their dwellings ﴿are signs﴾, great in themselves and numerous in their count. ﴿Will they not then listen?﴾: that is, will they not listen to these signs with the listening of reflection and taking warning?

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 32, verse 27:

﴿Do they not see?﴾ The discussion of this is like the discussion of ﴿Has it not become clear to them?﴾ That is, they are blind and do not witness it. ﴿That We drive the water﴾ by driving the clouds that carry it. It is said: We drive the water itself by means of torrents. It is also said: by making it flow in the rivers and from the springs, ﴿to the barren land﴾, that is, the land whose vegetation has been cut off (jurrizа), meaning it has been cut off either because of the lack of water or because it was grazed and cleared, as in al-Kashshaf (Zamakhshari's commentary).

In Majma' al-Bayan (of al-Tabrisi): "The barren land (al-ard al-juruz) is the dry land in which there is no vegetation, because the rains have ceased over it. From their saying: a jarrar sword (sayf jarraz), that is, a cutter that leaves nothing without cutting it; and a jarrar she-camel, when she eats everything and leaves nothing without cutting it with her mouth; and a man who is jaruz, that is, a great eater." The poet (al-rajiz) said:

*A cunning, voracious fellow, who weeps when he is hungry.*

Al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) said: "Juruz means the vegetation being cut off at its root. A land that is majruzah is one whose produce has been eaten. In a proverb: 'The hater will not be satisfied except with a uprooting' (bi-jarukah), that is, with total extirpation. The jarız is the severe cough, from which the meaning of juruz was derived, which is cutting with the sword." (End of quotation.) It is understood from what he said that juruz is applied to land whose vegetation has been cut off because it is not, by its nature, suited to growing plants, like salt flats. This is not appropriate here, given the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿so We bring forth thereby crops﴾. The apparent meaning is that what is intended is any land characterized by this attribute, whatever land it may be.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Hasan that it refers to villages between Yemen and Syria. He and Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Shaybah related from Ibn 'Abbas that it is a land in Yemen. Mujahid went to the view that it is not specified; a group related from him that he said: "The barren land is the one that does not produce plants; it is clearer and similar to other lands."

It is read as al-juruz (with a sukun on the ra'). The pronoun in ﴿thereby﴾ refers to the water. The statement is according to its apparent meaning in the view of the pious predecessors (al-salaf al-salih). The Ash'arites said: what is meant is ﴿so We bring forth by it (indahu)﴾. The word zar' (crops) is originally a verbal noun, used to refer to what is sown, and what is meant by it is what comes out by the rain in general, so it includes trees and other things. For this reason, the Exalted said: ﴿from which eat﴾, that is, from that produce, ﴿their livestock﴾, such as straw, green fodder, leaves, and some of the grains specific to them, ﴿and they themselves﴾, such as herbs and the grains that humans subsist on.

In al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit of Abu Hayyan): It is possible that by zar' is meant the well-known plant, and it was singled out for mention as an honor for it, and because it is the greatest of what is sought from plants. It is also possible that by it is meant plants in general. Livestock was mentioned first because their benefit is confined to this, whereas humans may feed on other things; and because their eating of it comes first, since they eat it before it bears fruit and produces its ear. It is said: this is so that it ascends from the lower to the higher, namely the children of Adam.

Abu Haywah and Abu Bakr, in one transmission, read ﴿yaʾkulu﴾ (with the yā' at the beginning, i.e., "it eats") instead.

﴿Will they not then see?﴾ That is: will they not see, and so not see that, in order to draw evidence from it for the perfection of His power, may He be exalted and glorified, and His bounty. The concluding word here is ﴿yubsirun (see)﴾ because what precedes it is visible, whereas in what precedes it the concluding word is ﴿yasma'un (hear)﴾ because what precedes it is audible. It is said: this is an ascent to a higher level in admonition, for emphasis in reminding and removing excuse.

Ibn Mas'ud read ﴿tubsirun﴾ with a upper tā' (second person).

**[Commentary of al-Alusi, Ruh al-Ma'ani, on Surah 32, verse 29]**

﴿Say﴾, as a rebuke to them and a confirmation of the truth: ﴿On the Day of Victory, the faith of those who disbelieved will not benefit them, nor will they be given respite﴾. Al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid that he said: "The Day of Victory is the Day of Resurrection." According to al-Bahr (Bahr al-Muhit), it is in the accusative case, governed by "will not benefit." The phrase "those who disbelieved" may refer either to those sayers who mocked, in which case the explicit noun is used in place of the pronoun to record their disbelief and to explain the reason for the ruling; or it may refer to them and others, in which case the ruling concerning those mockers is known by a demonstrative method. The meaning of His words, Exalted is He, ﴿nor will they be given respite﴾, is the continuation of the negation. Evidently the clause is coordinated with "will not benefit," and the qualification applies to it. The apparent sense of their question, ﴿When is this victory?﴾, requires an answer specifying the day asked about. However, since their purpose in asking about the time of the victory was to hasten it, in a manner of denial and mockery, they were answered according to what was known of their purpose. It is as if it were said to them: "Do not hasten it, and do not mock. I see you on that day, having arrived there, and having believed, but faith will not benefit you; and having sought respite to escape the punishment, but you will not be given respite." This is close to the rhetorical technique (al-uslub al-hakim, the wise manner of address), which is to answer a question in a way other than its literal form.

[Page 141]

Furthermore, interpreting "the Day of Victory" as the Day of Resurrection is evident on the view that "victory" means the settling of the dispute, since He, Glorified is He, said: ﴿Indeed, your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection﴾. It is hardly possible, however, on the view that it means victory over those sayers, since they were, by it, expecting victory and dominance over them in this world, as is evident from what you have heard from Mujahid. Accordingly, it has been said that the Day of Victory is the Day of Badr. This was related by al-Hakim, who declared it sound, and by al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il, from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. It has also been said that it is the Day of the Conquest of Makkah, and this is reported from al-Hasan and Mujahid. Both views face the objection that His words, ﴿On the Day of Victory, the faith of those who disbelieved will not benefit them﴾, apparently indicate that faith was not accepted from a disbeliever on that day, yet some people believed on the Day of Badr and their faith was accepted, and likewise on the Day of the Conquest of Makkah.

It has been answered that the relative pronoun on either view refers to those who were killed in disbelief on that day. So the meaning of "their faith will not benefit them" is that they have no faith by which they could be benefited. This is like the line of poetry: "On a well-trodden road whose landmarks cannot be followed."

Whether the reference is to a specific group who mocked or not, and whether His words "nor will they be given respite" are coordinated with the restricted clause or with the whole, the matter is the same, so consider this carefully.

It has been criticized: this is contrary to the apparent meaning. Also, that the Day of Victory is the Day of Badr is far from the Surah being Meccan, and likewise that it is the Day of the Conquest of Makkah. What further weakens this is the very small number of those killed on that day. Reflect on this.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 32, verse 30:**

﴿So turn away from them﴾, and do not concern yourself with their denial and mockery. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that this verse is abrogated (mansukh) by the verse of the sword. It is not hidden that it is possible the intended meaning is turning away from disputing with them, since it is of no benefit, or that it is restricted to a specific time, so abrogation (naskh, the cancellation of a ruling by a later revelation) is not definitively established.

﴿And wait﴾ for victory over them and their destruction. ﴿Indeed they too are waiting.﴾ The majority (al-Jumhur) said: that is, waiting for domination over you, as in His statement, ﴿So wait; indeed we are waiting with you﴾ [al-Tawbah: 52]. It has also been said: the more apparent view is that it means they are awaiting their own destruction, as in His statement, ﴿Do they await anything but that God should come to them in canopies of cloud...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 210], and close to this is what has been said: "And wait for Our punishment upon them; indeed they are waiting," meaning: this is their state, even if they do not perceive it, for their aforementioned hastening and their clinging to the disbelief and sins they are upon are equivalent to awaiting the punishment that will inevitably follow. Al-Yamani read «مُنْتَظَرُونَ» with a fatha on the ẓā' (muntaẓarūna, as a passive participle), meaning that they deserve to have their destruction awaited, or that the angels, peace be upon them, await it. The intended meaning is that they are certainly going to be destroyed.

"And from the door of allusion (ishara, an esoteric or intimated meaning of the verse)": His statement, ﴿You have, besides Him, neither any protector nor any intercessor﴾ [al-Sajdah: 4], contains an allusion that one should not turn toward means (asbab) or rely upon them. His glorified statement, ﴿He arranges the affair from the heaven to the earth﴾ [al-Sajdah: 5], contains an allusion that the management of servants has no effect in the presence of His management, glorified and exalted is He. So blessed is the one who is granted contentment with God's management, and who is independent of his own management. ﴿He who perfected everything He created﴾ [al-Sajdah: 7] contains guidance that no one should find any created thing ugly.

It is related that Noah, peace be upon him, spat on a mangy dog, so God made the dog speak, and it said: "O Noah, did you find fault with me, or did you find fault with my Creator?" Noah, peace be upon him, then wept over that for a long time.

So all things are good, each in its own place, and the variation is relative. And in His statement, ﴿and He began the creation of man from clay﴾ [al-Sajdah: 7] to the end of the verse, following His glorified statement, ﴿who perfected﴾ etc., there is an allusion to moving through the stages of goodness and ascending through its ladders. How great is the difference between clay and the human being, the hearing, seeing, knowing one, for man is the niche of the lights of the Essence and the Attributes, while clay in comparison to him is as nothing. ﴿Those who believe in Our signs are only those who, when they are reminded of them, fall down in prostration and glorify the praise of their Lord, and they are not arrogant﴾ [al-Sajdah: 15] is an allusion to the state of those of complete faith, and to the elevated standing of prostration, glorification, praise, and humility before His greatness, glorified and exalted is He. ﴿Their sides forsake their beds, they call upon their Lord in fear and hope﴾ [al-Sajdah: 16] is an allusion to their staying awake in intimate conversation with their Beloved, and contemplating His majesty and beauty. In His statement, ﴿and from what We have provided them﴾, i.e., from the knowledge and the various kinds of overflowing gifts, ﴿they spend﴾ [al-Sajdah: 16], there is an allusion to their perfecting others after their own perfection. The people (of Sufism) mentioned that "the lesser punishment" is greed for this world, and "the greater punishment" is the punishment resulting from that.

Some of them said: the first is the weariness in seeking this world, and the second is the scattering of the secret (the inner self). It has been said: the first is the deprivation of knowledge (ma'rifah), and the second is the veiling from witnessing the One Known. It has been said: the first is humiliation, and the second is abandonment. ﴿And We made from among them leaders guiding by Our command when they were patient, and they were certain of Our signs﴾ [al-Sajdah: 24] contains an allusion to the qualities that a guide ought to have: patience upon the hardships of worship and the various afflictions, restraining the self from the pleasures of desires, and certainty in the signs. Whoever claims to guide while not characterized by what has been mentioned is astray and misguiding. ﴿So turn away from them and wait; indeed they too are waiting﴾ [al-Sajdah: 30] contains an allusion that one should turn away from the deniers who mock the knowers and the travelers (on the spiritual path) when guidance and advice do not benefit them, and an allusion that they are certainly going to be destroyed. For the denial whose holder is not excused is a deadly poison and an arrow whose target is the vital spot. We seek refuge in God, exalted is He, from "al-ḥawr ba'd al-kawr" (returning to deficiency after having attained fullness), by the sanctity of His most noble Beloved, may God bless him and grant him peace, and his family and companions.
